title: The Limitation Act, 1908 (Bangladesh) - MCQ Bank for BJSC Preparation
note: Bangladesh continues to apply the Limitation Act, 1908 (Act IX of 1908) as amended, NOT India's Limitation Act 1963. Section numbers below follow the 1908 Act as generally cited in Bangladeshi practice. Always cross-check against the latest bare Act / Bangladesh Code before the exam, as some provisions have been amended post-1971.

mcqs.topic: Preliminary - S.2 Definitions
mcqs.question: Under S.2 of the Limitation Act, 1908, 'period of limitation' means:
options: The period of limitation computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act
The period fixed by the court in its discretion
The period agreed upon between the parties
The period fixed by the Government by notification
mcqs.answer: The period of limitation computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.2(j)

mcqs.topic: Preliminary - S.2 Definitions
mcqs.question: Under S.2 of the Limitation Act, 'prescribed period' means:
options: The period of limitation prescribed for a suit, appeal or application by the First Schedule
The period fixed by contract between the parties
The maximum period a court may extend limitation
The period prescribed by any special law only
mcqs.answer: The period of limitation prescribed for a suit, appeal or application by the First Schedule
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.2(i)

mcqs.topic: S.3 - Bar of Limitation
mcqs.question: S.3 of the Limitation Act provides that every suit instituted, appeal preferred, and application made after the prescribed period shall be dismissed, even though:
options: Limitation has not been set up as a defence
The defendant has expressly waived limitation in writing
Both parties consent to condonation
The suit involves a government party
mcqs.answer: Limitation has not been set up as a defence
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.3

mcqs.topic: S.3 - Bar of Limitation
mcqs.question: The bar of limitation under S.3 operates to bar:
options: Only the remedy, not the underlying right, in most cases
Both the right and the remedy in all cases
Only criminal proceedings
Only proceedings before tribunals
mcqs.answer: Only the remedy, not the underlying right, in most cases
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.3 - general principle

mcqs.topic: S.3 - Duty of Court
mcqs.question: It is well settled that the question of limitation under S.3 must be decided by the court:
options: Suo motu, even if not raised by any party
Only if raised by the defendant in written statement
Only if raised at the appellate stage
Only upon a separate application
mcqs.answer: Suo motu, even if not raised by any party
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.3 - judicial interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.4 - Expiry when court is closed
mcqs.question: Under S.4, where the prescribed period for any suit, appeal or application expires on a day when the court is closed, the suit, appeal or application may be instituted, preferred or made:
options: On the day the court reopens
Only within 7 days of reopening
It becomes automatically time-barred
Only with leave of the appellate court
mcqs.answer: On the day the court reopens
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.4

mcqs.topic: S.4 - Scope
mcqs.question: S.4 of the Limitation Act applies when the court is closed on the last day of the prescribed period. It does NOT apply where:
options: The court is open but the applicant was personally unable to attend
The court is closed due to a declared holiday
The court is closed due to vacation
The court is closed by administrative order
mcqs.answer: The court is open but the applicant was personally unable to attend
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.4 - interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.5 - Extension of Period
mcqs.question: S.5 of the Limitation Act permits condonation of delay in filing an appeal, or an application (other than one under Order XXI CPC), if the appellant/applicant satisfies the court that he had:
options: Sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or making the application within the prescribed period
Made a bona fide mistake of law only
Filed the appeal in a wrong forum
Obtained consent of the opposite party
mcqs.answer: Sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or making the application within the prescribed period
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.5

mcqs.topic: S.5 - Scope: Suits Excluded
mcqs.question: S.5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 does NOT apply to:
options: Suits
Appeals
Revisions
Applications for review of judgment
mcqs.answer: Suits
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.5 - proviso/scope

mcqs.topic: S.5 - Applications under Order XXI CPC
mcqs.question: S.5 of the Limitation Act expressly excludes from its benefit:
options: Applications under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure
Applications for leave to appeal
Applications for review of judgment
Applications for setting aside an ex-parte decree
mcqs.answer: Applications under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.5

mcqs.topic: S.5 - 'Sufficient Cause'
mcqs.question: 'Sufficient cause' under S.5 is generally construed by courts:
options: Liberally, to advance substantial justice, unless mala fide or gross negligence is shown
Strictly, so that delay of even one day is fatal
Only in favour of the government
Only where the delay is less than 30 days
mcqs.answer: Liberally, to advance substantial justice, unless mala fide or gross negligence is shown
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.5 - judicial interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.5 - Burden of Proof
mcqs.question: Under S.5, the burden of proving 'sufficient cause' for the delay lies on:
options: The appellant/applicant seeking condonation
The respondent opposing condonation
The court itself
Neither party; it is presumed in favour of condonation
mcqs.answer: The appellant/applicant seeking condonation
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.5

mcqs.topic: S.5 - Each Day's Delay
mcqs.question: Where there is inordinate delay in filing an appeal under S.5, courts generally require the applicant to explain:
options: Each day's delay, though not always with mathematical precision
Only the first day of delay
Only the last day of delay
No explanation is required if the appeal has merit
mcqs.answer: Each day's delay, though not always with mathematical precision
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.5 - judicial interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.6 - Legal Disability
mcqs.question: S.6 of the Limitation Act deals with the effect of legal disability, i.e., where a person entitled to institute a suit or make an application is, at the time from which the period of limitation is to be reckoned, a:
options: Minor, insane person, or idiot
Government servant
Foreign national
Undischarged bankrupt only
mcqs.answer: Minor, insane person, or idiot
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.6

mcqs.topic: S.6 - Effect of Legal Disability
mcqs.question: Under S.6, a person under legal disability may institute the suit or make the application after the disability ceases, within:
options: The same period as would otherwise have been allowed, computed from the cessation of disability
One year from cessation of disability, irrespective of the original period
Three years from cessation of disability in all cases
No limitation applies once disability ceases
mcqs.answer: The same period as would otherwise have been allowed, computed from the cessation of disability
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.6(1)

mcqs.topic: S.6 - Successive Disabilities
mcqs.question: Where a person under legal disability dies while still under disability without the disability ceasing, S.6(2)/(3) allows the legal representative to sue:
options: Within the same period after the disability would otherwise have ceased (subject to the proviso on successive disabilities)
Immediately, without any further limitation
Within 30 days of death only
Not at all, the right lapses on death
mcqs.answer: Within the same period after the disability would otherwise have ceased (subject to the proviso on successive disabilities)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.6(2)

mcqs.topic: S.7 - Disability of One of Several Persons
mcqs.question: Under S.7, where one of several persons jointly entitled to institute a suit or make an application is under a legal disability, time runs against all of them:
options: Unless discharge can be given without the concurrence of the person under disability
Immediately in every case
Only after all of them attain majority
Time never runs while any one of them is under disability
mcqs.answer: Unless discharge can be given without the concurrence of the person under disability
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.7

mcqs.topic: S.8 - Disability not to Extend beyond a Limit
mcqs.question: S.8 provides that nothing in S.6 or S.7 shall be deemed to extend the period of limitation for any suit or application beyond:
options: Three years from the cessation of disability or death, whichever first happens
One year in all circumstances
The original prescribed period only
There is no outer limit under S.8
mcqs.answer: Three years from the cessation of disability or death, whichever first happens
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.8

mcqs.topic: S.9 - Continuous Running of Time
mcqs.question: S.9 lays down the general principle that where time has begun to run, no subsequent disability or inability to sue stops it from running, except:
options: As expressly provided in the Act itself
In cases involving the government
In cases of fraud only
Where the cause of action is a continuing one
mcqs.answer: As expressly provided in the Act itself
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.9

mcqs.topic: S.9 - Once Time Begins to Run
mcqs.question: The principle under S.9 that 'once time begins to run, it runs continuously' means that even the death of a party or subsequent minority of a legal representative:
options: Does not stop the running of time already commenced, save as otherwise provided by the Act
Immediately stops limitation permanently
Restarts limitation from zero
Suspends limitation until a guardian is appointed
mcqs.answer: Does not stop the running of time already commenced, save as otherwise provided by the Act
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.9

mcqs.topic: S.10 - Suits against Trustees
mcqs.question: S.10 of the Limitation Act provides that no suit against a trustee or his representative to recover trust property, or for breach of trust, shall be barred by:
options: Any period of limitation, in respect of property vested in trust for a specific purpose
Any period exceeding 30 years
A period of more than 12 years
A period of more than 6 years
mcqs.answer: Any period of limitation, in respect of property vested in trust for a specific purpose
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.10

mcqs.topic: S.10 - Rationale
mcqs.question: The rationale for S.10 exempting certain trust suits from limitation is that a trustee holding property for a specific purpose:
options: Cannot be allowed to plead limitation against his own beneficiary in respect of that property
Is treated the same as any ordinary debtor
Enjoys absolute ownership after 12 years
Is protected only if the trust is registered
mcqs.answer: Cannot be allowed to plead limitation against his own beneficiary in respect of that property
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.10 - rationale

mcqs.topic: S.11 - Suits on Foreign Contracts
mcqs.question: S.11 deals with suits on contracts entered into by persons resident outside the country (formerly 'British India'). It provides that such suits are not barred by reason of the fact that:
options: The contract was, according to the law of the foreign country, barred by limitation there
The contract was oral rather than written
The parties were non-citizens
The contract was for an illegal purpose
mcqs.answer: The contract was, according to the law of the foreign country, barred by limitation there
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.11

mcqs.topic: S.12 - Exclusion of Time in Legal Proceedings
mcqs.question: Under S.12(1), in computing the period of limitation for any suit, appeal or application, the day from which such period is to be reckoned shall be:
options: Excluded
Included
Counted twice
Determined by the court's discretion
mcqs.answer: Excluded
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.12(1)

mcqs.topic: S.12(2) - Time for Obtaining Copy
mcqs.question: Under S.12(2), in computing the period of limitation for an appeal, application for leave to appeal, or application for revision or review of judgment, the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the:
options: Decree, sentence or order appealed from or sought to be revised/reviewed shall be excluded
Plaint filed by the opposite party shall be excluded
Written statement shall be excluded
Entire case record shall be excluded
mcqs.answer: Decree, sentence or order appealed from or sought to be revised/reviewed shall be excluded
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.12(2)

mcqs.topic: S.12(3) - Copy of Judgment for Appeal against Decree
mcqs.question: Under S.12(3), where an appeal is against a decree, the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the judgment on which the decree is founded shall also be:
options: Excluded, in addition to the time for obtaining the decree copy
Included as part of the limitation period
Irrelevant, since only the decree copy matters
Counted only if requested within 7 days of judgment
mcqs.answer: Excluded, in addition to the time for obtaining the decree copy
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.12(3)

mcqs.topic: S.12 - Scenario
mcqs.question: A judgment is delivered on 1 January. The certified copy of the decree is applied for on 3 January and ready for collection on 20 January. For computing the limitation period for appeal, the period from 3 January to 20 January is:
options: Excluded under S.12(2) as time requisite for obtaining the copy
Included in full
Excluded only if delay is condoned under S.5
Irrelevant since S.12 applies only to suits
mcqs.answer: Excluded under S.12(2) as time requisite for obtaining the copy
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.12(2) - application

mcqs.topic: S.13 - Suits by Paupers
mcqs.question: S.13 excludes, in computing the period of limitation for a suit, the time during which the plaintiff has been prosecuting with due diligence:
options: An application for leave to sue as a pauper (in forma pauperis)
A criminal complaint on the same facts
A departmental appeal
An application for anticipatory bail
mcqs.answer: An application for leave to sue as a pauper (in forma pauperis)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.13

mcqs.topic: S.14 - Bona Fide Proceedings in Wrong Court
mcqs.question: S.14 excludes, in computing the period of limitation, the time during which the plaintiff has been prosecuting with due diligence another civil proceeding, whether in a court of first instance or appeal, against the defendant, where such proceeding is founded upon the same cause of action and is prosecuted:
options: In good faith in a court which, from defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature, is unable to entertain it
In bad faith to harass the defendant
In a criminal court
Before an administrative tribunal only
mcqs.answer: In good faith in a court which, from defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature, is unable to entertain it
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.14(1)

mcqs.topic: S.14 - 'Good Faith'
mcqs.question: Under S.14, 'good faith' requires that the proceeding be prosecuted with:
options: Due care and attention
Absolute certainty of success
Consent of the defendant
Legal advice from a Senior Advocate
mcqs.answer: Due care and attention
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.14, read with S.2 definition of 'good faith'

mcqs.topic: S.14 - Applicability to Execution Proceedings
mcqs.question: S.14(2) extends the principle of exclusion of time to:
options: Applications, including applications for execution of a decree
Only original suits
Only first appeals
Only criminal revisions
mcqs.answer: Applications, including applications for execution of a decree
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.14(2)

mcqs.topic: S.14 - Scenario
mcqs.question: A plaintiff files a suit in Court A, which is later found to lack pecuniary jurisdiction, and the plaint is returned. He promptly re-files in Court B, which has jurisdiction. The time spent bona fide in Court A is:
options: Excluded under S.14 while computing limitation for the suit in Court B
Not excluded, as filing in the wrong court is always negligence
Excluded only if Court A explicitly certifies good faith
Excluded only for appeals, not suits
mcqs.answer: Excluded under S.14 while computing limitation for the suit in Court B
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.14 - application

mcqs.topic: S.15 - Exclusion of Time During Stay/Injunction
mcqs.question: S.15(1) excludes, in computing the period of limitation for a suit or application, the time during which the institution of the suit or execution of the decree has been stayed by:
options: An injunction or order of a court
A private agreement between the parties only
A newspaper notice
The plaintiff's own unilateral decision
mcqs.answer: An injunction or order of a court
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.15(1)

mcqs.topic: S.15 - Notice Requirement before Suit
mcqs.question: S.15(2) excludes, in computing the period of limitation for a suit, the period of notice required by law or contract to be given before instituting the suit, in cases where such notice has been:
options: Given
Waived by the defendant
Published in a gazette
Served on a third party
mcqs.answer: Given
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.15(2)

mcqs.topic: S.15 - Sanction/Consent Requirement
mcqs.question: S.15 also excludes time during which the plaintiff is prohibited by law from instituting a suit or application, such as while awaiting:
options: Statutory sanction or consent required before suing (e.g., against a public officer)
The defendant's convenience
A change in government
Publication of a new bare act
mcqs.answer: Statutory sanction or consent required before suing (e.g., against a public officer)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.15

mcqs.topic: S.15 - Execution Stayed by Injunction
mcqs.question: Where execution of a decree is stayed by an order of a superior court pending appeal, the period during which the stay operates is, for purposes of a subsequent execution application:
options: Excluded under S.15(1)
Included and counted against the decree-holder
Doubled as a penalty
Irrelevant since execution has no limitation
mcqs.answer: Excluded under S.15(1)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.15(1)

mcqs.topic: S.16 - Effect of Death Before Accrual
mcqs.question: S.16 deals with the situation where a person dies before the right to sue accrues, or where a person against whom the right to sue would have accrued dies before it accrues. In such cases, the period of limitation is computed:
options: From the time when there is a legal representative capable of suing or being sued
From the date of death itself, regardless of representation
From the date the right would have accrued to the deceased, with no adjustment
There is no limitation once the original party has died
mcqs.answer: From the time when there is a legal representative capable of suing or being sued
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.16

mcqs.topic: S.17 - Effect of Fraud
mcqs.question: S.17 provides that where a suit or application is based upon the fraud of the defendant or his agent, or where the knowledge of the right or title on which a suit or application is founded is fraudulently concealed, the period of limitation shall not begin to run until:
options: The plaintiff/applicant has discovered the fraud, or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it
The defendant confesses the fraud in writing
A criminal court convicts the defendant of fraud
The fraud is registered with the Sub-Registrar
mcqs.answer: The plaintiff/applicant has discovered the fraud, or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.17

mcqs.topic: S.17 - Protection of Bona Fide Purchasers
mcqs.question: The proviso to S.17 protects, notwithstanding the fraud, the rights of:
options: A purchaser in good faith for valuable consideration who is not a party to the fraud
The defendant who committed the fraud
The plaintiff's agent
Any third party regardless of knowledge of the fraud
mcqs.answer: A purchaser in good faith for valuable consideration who is not a party to the fraud
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.17 proviso

mcqs.topic: S.18 - Effect of Acknowledgment
mcqs.question: S.18 provides that where, before the expiration of the prescribed period, an acknowledgment of liability in respect of a right has been made in writing signed by the party against whom the right is claimed, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed:
options: From the time when the acknowledgment was so signed
From the original date the right accrued
From the date the acknowledgment is registered
Only if the acknowledgment is notarized
mcqs.answer: From the time when the acknowledgment was so signed
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.18

mcqs.topic: S.18 - Requirements of Valid Acknowledgment
mcqs.question: For an acknowledgment under S.18 to give rise to a fresh period of limitation, it must:
options: Be made before expiry of the then-current limitation period and be in writing signed by the party or his agent
Be made after the limitation period has already expired
Be oral but witnessed by two persons
Specify the exact amount due, without which it is invalid
mcqs.answer: Be made before expiry of the then-current limitation period and be in writing signed by the party or his agent
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.18

mcqs.topic: S.18 - Acknowledgment after Expiry
mcqs.question: An acknowledgment of liability made AFTER the prescribed period of limitation has already expired:
options: Does not give a fresh starting point of limitation under S.18
Automatically revives the time-barred claim
Extends limitation by exactly one more year
Is treated the same as a fresh contract in all respects
mcqs.answer: Does not give a fresh starting point of limitation under S.18
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.18 - interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.18 - Implied Acknowledgment
mcqs.question: Under S.18, an acknowledgment need not specify the exact figure or amount due; it is sufficient if the writing:
options: Admits a jural relationship (existence of the liability), even without quantifying it
Is signed by a witness only
Contains the word 'acknowledgment' expressly
Is registered with the relevant Registrar
mcqs.answer: Admits a jural relationship (existence of the liability), even without quantifying it
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.18 - judicial interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.19 - Effect of Part Payment
mcqs.question: S.19 provides that where part payment of the principal, or interest on a debt, is made before the expiration of the prescribed period by the person liable to pay it, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the payment was made, provided that:
options: An acknowledgment of the payment appears in the handwriting of, or in a writing signed by, the person making it
The payment is made in cash only
The payment is at least half of the total debt
The creditor issues a formal receipt on stamp paper
mcqs.answer: An acknowledgment of the payment appears in the handwriting of, or in a writing signed by, the person making it
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.19

mcqs.topic: S.19 vs S.20 - Payment by Agent
mcqs.question: S.20 extends the benefit of S.19 (part payment) and S.18 (acknowledgment) to acknowledgments/payments made by an agent duly authorised in this behalf, and also deals with payment by:
options: One of several joint contractors, partners, executors or mortgagees, in certain circumstances
A total stranger to the transaction
The court itself
A witness to the original contract
mcqs.answer: One of several joint contractors, partners, executors or mortgagees, in certain circumstances
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.20

mcqs.topic: S.21 - Effect of Adding New Parties
mcqs.question: S.21 provides that where a new plaintiff or defendant is substituted or added in a suit, the suit is, as regards such party, deemed to have been instituted:
options: When such party was so made a party, unless the court otherwise directs on grounds of mistake made in good faith
From the date of the original institution of the suit in every case
From the date of judgment
There is no limitation issue once a party is added by court order
mcqs.answer: When such party was so made a party, unless the court otherwise directs on grounds of mistake made in good faith
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.21

mcqs.topic: S.22 - Continuing Breach/Tort
mcqs.question: S.22 provides that in the case of a continuing breach of contract, and in the case of a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run:
options: At every moment of time during which the breach or tort continues
Only once, at the time the breach first occurred
Only at the time the breach ceases
Only if the plaintiff issues a legal notice
mcqs.answer: At every moment of time during which the breach or tort continues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.22

mcqs.topic: S.23 - Suits for Compensation for Non-Actionable Acts
mcqs.question: S.23 deals with suits for compensation for an act which does not give rise to a cause of action unless some specific injury actually results therefrom. In such cases, the period of limitation is computed from the time when the injury:
options: Results
The act was committed, regardless of resulting injury
Is first threatened
Is reported to police
mcqs.answer: Results
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.23

mcqs.topic: S.24 - Computation of Time in Instruments
mcqs.question: S.24 provides that in computing time appointed or allowed by any 'agreement or order of Court, or by any rule of law', for doing an act, the time so appointed or allowed shall be computed:
options: In like manner as periods prescribed by the Act itself for suits/applications
In calendar months only, never in days
By excluding all holidays automatically
By reference to the Gregorian calendar exclusively, ignoring the Bangla calendar
mcqs.answer: In like manner as periods prescribed by the Act itself for suits/applications
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.24

mcqs.topic: S.25 - Acquisition of Easements
mcqs.question: S.25 of the Limitation Act deals with the acquisition of a right to easement (e.g., right of way, light and air) by:
options: Peaceable and open enjoyment as an easement, without interruption, for the prescribed period
Registration with the Sub-Registrar alone
Mere oral permission of the servient owner
A single instance of use
mcqs.answer: Peaceable and open enjoyment as an easement, without interruption, for the prescribed period
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.25

mcqs.topic: S.25 - Nature of Enjoyment Required
mcqs.question: For acquisition of an easementary right under S.25, the enjoyment must be:
options: As of right, peaceable, and open (nec vi, nec clam, nec precario)
Secret and forcible
Permissive throughout
Interrupted periodically by the dominant owner
mcqs.answer: As of right, peaceable, and open (nec vi, nec clam, nec precario)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.25 - interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.26 - Exclusion in Favour of Reversioner
mcqs.question: S.26 provides that where any land or water upon, over or from which any easement has been enjoyed is held under an interest for life, or in tenancy for a term of years, the time of the enjoyment during the continuance of such interest or term shall be excluded in computing the period applicable to the case, where the claim is resisted by a person entitled to the interest in reversion, provided the claim is resisted within:
options: Three years next after the termination of such interest or term
One year of enjoyment commencing
Ten years unconditionally
No time limit applies to a reversioner
mcqs.answer: Three years next after the termination of such interest or term
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.26

mcqs.topic: S.27 - Extinguishment of Right
mcqs.question: S.27 of the Limitation Act provides a striking exception to the general rule that limitation bars only the remedy: at the determination of the period limited by the Act to a person for instituting a suit for possession of any property, his right to such property:
options: Is extinguished
Merely becomes unenforceable but survives in substance
Is transferred automatically to the State
Is suspended pending review
mcqs.answer: Is extinguished
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.27

mcqs.topic: S.27 - Significance
mcqs.question: S.27 is significant because it is one of the few provisions under which limitation extinguishes the substantive right itself (not merely the remedy), making it central to law of:
options: Adverse possession
Contract formation
Criminal procedure
Company incorporation
mcqs.answer: Adverse possession
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.27 - interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.28 - Repealed Provision
mcqs.question: Historically, S.28 of the Limitation Act, 1908 dealt with:
options: Bar of suit not affecting extinguishment of right in certain cases (later substantially covered/refined by S.27's scope and subsequent amendments)
Definitions of court fee
Arbitration proceedings
Criminal appeals
mcqs.answer: Bar of suit not affecting extinguishment of right in certain cases (later substantially covered/refined by S.27's scope and subsequent amendments)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - historical note; verify current status against latest bare Act

mcqs.topic: S.29 - Savings
mcqs.question: S.29 of the Limitation Act is a savings clause providing that nothing in the Act shall affect S.25 of the Contract Act, or:
options: Any special or local law prescribing a period of limitation different from that in the Schedule, subject to specified sections applying unless expressly excluded
Any provision of criminal law
Any provision of the Constitution
Any provision of company law only
mcqs.answer: Any special or local law prescribing a period of limitation different from that in the Schedule, subject to specified sections applying unless expressly excluded
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.29

mcqs.topic: S.29(2) - Special/Local Law
mcqs.question: Under S.29(2), where any special or local law prescribes a period of limitation different from the period prescribed by the First Schedule, the provisions of S.3 shall apply as if such period were prescribed by the Schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed by such special/local law, the provisions of Ss.4 to 25 shall apply:
options: Only insofar as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or local law
In no circumstances
Automatically without exception
Only if the special law is enacted before 1908
mcqs.answer: Only insofar as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or local law
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.29(2)

mcqs.topic: S.29(2) - Scenario
mcqs.question: A special statute (e.g., a Rent Control or Motor Vehicles-type law) prescribes its own limitation period for filing a claim and is silent on whether S.5 (condonation of delay) applies. In such a case, courts generally hold that S.5:
options: Applies by virtue of S.29(2), unless expressly or by necessary implication excluded by the special law
Never applies to any special law
Applies only if the special law is a Presidential Order
Applies only to criminal special laws
mcqs.answer: Applies by virtue of S.29(2), unless expressly or by necessary implication excluded by the special law
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.29(2) - interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.30 - Application to Existing Suits
mcqs.question: Provisions in the Limitation Act dealing with the transition/application of the Act to suits, appeals, and applications pending or arising at the time of its commencement are generally addressed under transitional provisions such as:
options: S.30 and related savings/transitional sections
S.5 exclusively
S.27 exclusively
The Preamble alone, with no operative effect
mcqs.answer: S.30 and related savings/transitional sections
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - transitional provisions; verify exact section number in current bare Act

mcqs.topic: S.31 - Provisions as to Barred Debts
mcqs.question: S.31 clarifies that nothing in the Act shall:
options: Revive a right of action already barred by any enactment repealed by the Act
Bar any right of action that survives independently
Extend limitation for suits by the government
Apply to any suit filed before 1908
mcqs.answer: Revive a right of action already barred by any enactment repealed by the Act
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.31

mcqs.topic: S.32 - Repeal
mcqs.question: S.32 of the Limitation Act, 1908 is essentially:
options: A repealing provision, repealing earlier limitation enactments
The main charging section prescribing limitation for suits
A provision dealing with court fees
A definition clause
mcqs.answer: A repealing provision, repealing earlier limitation enactments
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.32

mcqs.topic: General - Right to Sue Accrues
mcqs.question: As a general principle under the Limitation Act, the period of limitation for most suits begins to run from the date when:
options: The right to sue first accrues (cause of action arises)
The plaint is drafted
The defendant is served with summons
The court takes cognizance
mcqs.answer: The right to sue first accrues (cause of action arises)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general principle underlying Schedule I

mcqs.topic: General - Limitation vs Jurisdiction
mcqs.question: A plea of limitation under the Limitation Act is a plea:
options: Going to the root of the maintainability of the suit and can be raised at any stage, even in second appeal
That can only be raised in the written statement, never later
That is waived if not raised at the first hearing
Available only to the plaintiff, never the defendant
mcqs.answer: Going to the root of the maintainability of the suit and can be raised at any stage, even in second appeal
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - S.3 interpretation

mcqs.topic: General - Limitation and Res Judicata
mcqs.question: Where a suit is dismissed as time-barred, such a decision, if it attains finality, operates as res judicata on the question of limitation because it is a decision:
options: On a matter of substance, not merely procedure
That can be reopened at will in a fresh suit
Binding only on the plaintiff, not privies
Never appealable
mcqs.answer: On a matter of substance, not merely procedure
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general principle, cf. S.11 CPC

mcqs.topic: Scenario - S.18 Acknowledgment
mcqs.question: A debtor, in a letter to the creditor written 2 years into a 3-year limitation period for a simple debt, writes: 'I acknowledge I owe you money and will pay soon.' This letter, signed by the debtor:
options: Constitutes a valid acknowledgment under S.18, giving a fresh 3-year period from the date of the letter
Has no legal effect since it does not mention the exact sum
Is invalid because it must be registered
Extends limitation only by 1 year
mcqs.answer: Constitutes a valid acknowledgment under S.18, giving a fresh 3-year period from the date of the letter
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.18 - application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - S.19 Part Payment
mcqs.question: A borrower makes a partial repayment of a loan and the payment is duly endorsed on the promissory note in the borrower's own handwriting, within the original limitation period. This has the effect of:
options: Starting a fresh period of limitation from the date of such payment under S.19
Having no effect on limitation at all
Discharging the entire debt automatically
Converting the debt into a decree
mcqs.answer: Starting a fresh period of limitation from the date of such payment under S.19
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.19 - application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - S.6 Minor Plaintiff
mcqs.question: A cause of action to recover property accrues when X is 12 years old (a minor). X attains majority at 18. Under S.6, the limitation period for X's suit runs:
options: From the date X attains majority (age 18), for the same period otherwise allowed
From the date the cause of action accrued (age 12), with no relief for minority
Never, since minors can never be barred
From the date of X's marriage, regardless of age
mcqs.answer: From the date X attains majority (age 18), for the same period otherwise allowed
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.6 - application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - S.17 Fraudulent Concealment
mcqs.question: A vendor fraudulently conceals a defect in title while selling property. The purchaser discovers the fraud only 5 years later. Under S.17, limitation for a suit based on this fraud begins to run from:
options: The date the purchaser discovered the fraud (or could have discovered it with reasonable diligence)
The date of the original sale, regardless of concealment
The date of the vendor's death
There is no limitation once fraud is proved
mcqs.answer: The date the purchaser discovered the fraud (or could have discovered it with reasonable diligence)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.17 - application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - S.22 Continuing Wrong
mcqs.question: A neighbour continues to obstruct a right of way, day after day, for several years. For a suit for injunction/damages, S.22 provides that a fresh cause of action arises:
options: Every day the obstruction continues
Only on the first day the obstruction began
Only when the obstruction is removed
Only once, on the day of filing the suit
mcqs.answer: Every day the obstruction continues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.22 - application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - S.14 Bona Fide Litigation
mcqs.question: A plaintiff files execution proceedings in a court that later turns out to lack territorial jurisdiction, and diligently pursues that application for 2 years before it is dismissed for want of jurisdiction. He then promptly files in the correct court. Under S.14(2), the 2 years spent in the wrong court will be:
options: Excluded from the limitation period for the fresh execution application
Counted against him fully
Excluded only if he pays additional court fees
Irrelevant since S.14 does not apply to execution
mcqs.answer: Excluded from the limitation period for the fresh execution application
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.14(2) - application

mcqs.topic: S.6-8 - Successive Legal Disabilities
mcqs.question: If a person is a minor and subsequently, upon attaining majority but before the disability period runs out fully, becomes of unsound mind (a second disability), S.8 ensures that in no case shall the total extension exceed:
options: Three years from cessation of the disability or death, whichever first happens, notwithstanding successive disabilities
An unlimited period, since disabilities are cumulative without limit
Six years flat
The extension is void and time runs from the original accrual regardless
mcqs.answer: Three years from cessation of the disability or death, whichever first happens, notwithstanding successive disabilities
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.8

mcqs.topic: S.5 - Applicability to Cross-Objections
mcqs.question: Courts have generally held that the benefit of S.5 (condonation of delay) is available to a memorandum of cross-objections, since a cross-objection is treated, for limitation purposes, akin to:
options: An appeal
A fresh suit
A criminal complaint
An execution petition under Order XXI
mcqs.answer: An appeal
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.5 - interpretation with Order XLI Rule 22 CPC

mcqs.topic: S.5 - 'Applicant Appearing in Person'
mcqs.question: Explanation to S.5 clarifies that the fact that an applicant/appellant was misled by any order, practice or judgment of the High Court in ascertaining or computing the prescribed period may be:
options: Sufficient cause for condonation of delay
Never sufficient cause
Relevant only for government litigants
Relevant only in criminal appeals
mcqs.answer: Sufficient cause for condonation of delay
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.5 - Explanation

mcqs.topic: S.12 - Time for Obtaining Copy of Order Refusing Leave
mcqs.question: The exclusion of time under S.12(2) for obtaining a copy applies to appeals, and applications for leave to appeal, revision, or:
options: Review of judgment
Filing a written statement
Filing an interlocutory application for injunction
Filing a plaint for the first time
mcqs.answer: Review of judgment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.12(2)

mcqs.topic: S.12 - Delay Attributable to Court
mcqs.question: Under S.12, if there is delay by the court establishment in preparing/certifying a copy applied for promptly and diligently, such delay is:
options: Excluded from limitation, as it is 'time requisite' regardless of court delay
Counted fully against the applicant
Split 50-50 between applicant and respondent
Excluded only if the applicant files a complaint against the court staff
mcqs.answer: Excluded from limitation, as it is 'time requisite' regardless of court delay
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.12(2) - interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.15 - Suit against Public Officer (Notice)
mcqs.question: Where a statute (e.g., in suits against the government or public officers) requires a mandatory notice period before suit (such as under S.80 CPC), the notice period is:
options: Excluded from the limitation period for the suit under S.15(2)
Included, effectively shortening the plaintiff's time to sue
Doubled automatically
Irrelevant to limitation altogether
mcqs.answer: Excluded from the limitation period for the suit under S.15(2)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.15(2)

mcqs.topic: S.16 - Legal Representative Suing
mcqs.question: S.16 ensures that limitation does not unfairly run against an estate where, at the moment a right to sue would have accrued, there is no person capable of suing because the potential plaintiff has just died; time begins only when there exists:
options: A legal representative capable of instituting such suit or application
A registered will
A probate granted by the High Court Division
A succession certificate obtained within 90 days
mcqs.answer: A legal representative capable of instituting such suit or application
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.16

mcqs.topic: S.19 - Nature of Acknowledgment of Payment
mcqs.question: Under S.19, for a part-payment to extend limitation, the acknowledgment of such payment must appear in the handwriting of, or be signed by, the person making the payment; a mere entry in the creditor's own account book, unsigned by the debtor, is:
options: Generally insufficient by itself to satisfy S.19, absent the debtor's own acknowledgment
Always sufficient regardless of who wrote it
Sufficient only if notarized
Sufficient if witnessed by two independent persons
mcqs.answer: Generally insufficient by itself to satisfy S.19, absent the debtor's own acknowledgment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.19 - interpretation

mcqs.topic: S.20 - Effect on Co-Contractors
mcqs.question: S.20 provides that where there are two or more joint contractors, and one of them makes payment/acknowledgment, such payment/acknowledgment shall NOT bind the others merely by virtue of their joint liability, unless:
options: It is proved that the payment was made on behalf of, or the acknowledgment was made for, all the joint contractors, or the other conditions of S.20 are satisfied
It is always binding on all joint contractors automatically
It is registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies
None of the above; S.20 does not deal with joint contractors at all
mcqs.answer: It is proved that the payment was made on behalf of, or the acknowledgment was made for, all the joint contractors, or the other conditions of S.20 are satisfied
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.20

mcqs.topic: S.21 - Amendment Relating Back
mcqs.question: As an exception to the general rule in S.21 (that adding a party is deemed to be a fresh institution as against that party), the court may direct that the suit be deemed instituted, as against the new party, on the earlier (original) date, if it is satisfied that the omission to include that party was:
options: Due to a mistake made in good faith
A deliberate strategic choice by the plaintiff
Caused by the defendant's own fraud only
Never permissible under any circumstances
mcqs.answer: Due to a mistake made in good faith
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.21 proviso

mcqs.topic: S.22 - Continuing Breach of Contract
mcqs.question: An employer fails, month after month, to pay an agreed monthly allowance under a continuing contract. Under S.22, limitation for a suit to recover the arrears:
options: Runs afresh each month in respect of the instalment falling due that month
Runs only once, from the date of the very first default
Never begins to run so long as the contract subsists
Applies only to torts, not to contracts
mcqs.answer: Runs afresh each month in respect of the instalment falling due that month
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.22 - application

mcqs.topic: S.25 - Interruption of Easement Enjoyment
mcqs.question: Under the Explanation to S.25, an enjoyment of an easement is not deemed to be interrupted merely because it is:
options: Suspended or altered temporarily, as e.g. by repairs, without any deliberate act of the servient owner amounting to obstruction acquiesced in for one year after notice
Continuous for over 20 years
Recorded in a registered deed
Practised only during daylight hours
mcqs.answer: Suspended or altered temporarily, as e.g. by repairs, without any deliberate act of the servient owner amounting to obstruction acquiesced in for one year after notice
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.25 - Explanation

mcqs.topic: S.27 - Adverse Possession Requirement
mcqs.question: For S.27 to operate and extinguish the true owner's title, the possession of the person in wrongful occupation must be:
options: Open, continuous, hostile/adverse to the true owner's title, and for the full statutory period
Secret and occasional
With the express permission of the true owner
For any period, however short
mcqs.answer: Open, continuous, hostile/adverse to the true owner's title, and for the full statutory period
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.27 - judicial interpretation of adverse possession

mcqs.topic: General - Permissive Possession
mcqs.question: Possession that begins permissively (e.g., as a licensee, tenant, or with the owner's consent) does NOT become adverse for purposes of S.27 unless and until:
options: There is a clear and hostile assertion of an independent title, brought to the knowledge of the true owner
Ten years elapse automatically
The occupant pays property tax
The occupant builds a permanent structure
mcqs.answer: There is a clear and hostile assertion of an independent title, brought to the knowledge of the true owner
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.27 - judicial interpretation

mcqs.topic: General - Limitation is a Procedural Law
mcqs.question: As a general rule of statutory interpretation, the law of limitation is regarded as:
options: Procedural (lex fori), though S.27 is a notable substantive exception
Wholly substantive with no procedural character
Part of criminal law only
Not applicable to civil suits at all
mcqs.answer: Procedural (lex fori), though S.27 is a notable substantive exception
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general principle

mcqs.topic: General - Retrospective Operation
mcqs.question: Where a new limitation law shortens the period previously available and comes into force while an old cause of action is still alive, courts generally hold that a reasonable time from the commencement of the new law must be given, applying the principle that:
options: Limitation statutes should not be construed so as to defeat a vested right of action without reasonable opportunity to sue
The new law always applies retrospectively without exception
The old law continues to apply forever
Such statutes have no effect on pending rights
mcqs.answer: Limitation statutes should not be construed so as to defeat a vested right of action without reasonable opportunity to sue
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general principle of interpretation

mcqs.topic: General - Limitation and Estoppel
mcqs.question: Parties cannot, by their own agreement, contract out of or extend the statutory period of limitation prescribed by the Act, because limitation is considered:
options: A matter of public policy, not merely private right
Purely a matter of private contract
Applicable only if pleaded by both parties jointly
Waivable by mutual consent at any time
mcqs.answer: A matter of public policy, not merely private right
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.3 - general principle

mcqs.topic: General - Amendment of Plaint and Limitation
mcqs.question: Where a plaintiff seeks to amend the plaint to introduce a wholly new cause of action after the limitation period for that new cause has expired, courts generally:
options: Refuse the amendment, since it would defeat the law of limitation
Always allow it if court fee is paid
Allow it automatically since amendments relate back to the original filing in all cases
Treat it as irrelevant to limitation
mcqs.answer: Refuse the amendment, since it would defeat the law of limitation
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general principle, cf. Order VI Rule 17 CPC

mcqs.topic: General - Limitation for Execution
mcqs.question: Applications for execution of decrees are, for limitation purposes, governed primarily by the relevant Article of the Third Division (Applications) of the First Schedule, and S.5's benefit (condonation) is, by the express terms of S.5, generally:
options: Not available for applications under Order XXI CPC (execution applications)
Fully available without restriction
Available only for decree-holders, not judgment-debtors
Available only in money decrees
mcqs.answer: Not available for applications under Order XXI CPC (execution applications)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.5 proviso

mcqs.topic: General - Limitation for Arbitration
mcqs.question: In the context of arbitration, the general principle (also reflected in the Limitation Act's scheme via S.29(2) and the Arbitration Act) is that the Limitation Act applies to arbitrations:
options: As it applies to court proceedings, so far as it can be made applicable
Never applies to arbitration in any manner
Applies only to international arbitration
Applies only after an arbitral award is passed
mcqs.answer: As it applies to court proceedings, so far as it can be made applicable
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.29(2) read with Arbitration Act

mcqs.topic: General - Suit for Declaration
mcqs.question: In a suit for a declaration of title, if a plaintiff is also in possession, the cause of action for limitation is generally treated as:
options: Recurring/continuing while the cloud on title persists, though this is fact-specific
Fixed permanently only at the moment the cloud arose, with no exceptions
Irrelevant, since declaratory suits have no limitation
Always barred after exactly 1 year
mcqs.answer: Recurring/continuing while the cloud on title persists, though this is fact-specific
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general interpretation applicable to declaratory suits

mcqs.topic: General - Time Barred Debt as Consideration
mcqs.question: A time-barred debt, though not recoverable by suit, may still serve as valid consideration for a fresh promise to pay under contract law principles, illustrating the maxim that limitation:
options: Bars the remedy but does not extinguish the underlying obligation (except where S.27 applies)
Extinguishes the debt completely in every case
Converts the debt into a criminal liability
Has no relevance to contract law
mcqs.answer: Bars the remedy but does not extinguish the underlying obligation (except where S.27 applies)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general principle, cf. Contract Act S.25(3)

mcqs.topic: General - Counter-claim and Limitation
mcqs.question: For purposes of limitation, a counter-claim filed by a defendant is generally treated as a cross-suit, and limitation is computed with reference to the date on which the counter-claim is:
options: Filed, and not the date of the original plaint (unless the applicable law provides otherwise)
Filed, but backdated automatically to the date of the plaint in every case
Deemed irrelevant since counter-claims have no limitation
Computed from the date of the written statement, always
mcqs.answer: Filed, and not the date of the original plaint (unless the applicable law provides otherwise)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general principle, cf. Order VIII CPC

mcqs.topic: General - Limitation and Void/Voidable Transactions
mcqs.question: For a suit to set aside a voidable transaction (e.g., a voidable sale), limitation typically begins to run from the date the plaintiff:
options: First had knowledge of the facts entitling him to avoid the transaction
Was born
The transaction was registered, regardless of knowledge
The other party died
mcqs.answer: First had knowledge of the facts entitling him to avoid the transaction
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general principle applicable to voidable transactions

mcqs.topic: General - Void Transactions
mcqs.question: Unlike a voidable transaction, a suit for a declaration that a transaction is void ab initio is generally treated, for limitation purposes, as one where the cause of action:
options: May be treated as continuing or as arising afresh whenever the void document is sought to be enforced, subject to case-specific facts
Never has any limitation issue at all under any circumstances
Must always be filed within 30 days
Is governed exclusively by criminal law
mcqs.answer: May be treated as continuing or as arising afresh whenever the void document is sought to be enforced, subject to case-specific facts
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general interpretation

mcqs.topic: General - Interpretation Rule: Beneficial Construction
mcqs.question: As a rule of interpretation, provisions of the Limitation Act that shorten the time for enforcing a right are construed strictly, while provisions like S.5 that allow condonation of delay are, in the interest of substantial justice, generally construed:
options: Liberally
Strictly against the applicant always
In favour of the State only
So as to defeat the appeal wherever possible
mcqs.answer: Liberally
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - rule of interpretation

mcqs.topic: General - Limitation and Jurisdictional Bar
mcqs.question: A decree passed by a court in a suit that was, in fact, barred by limitation, but where the point of limitation was neither raised nor considered, is:
options: Not automatically a nullity for want of jurisdiction merely because it is barred by limitation, though it may be erroneous and open to appeal/revision
Always void ab initio for want of jurisdiction
Incapable of execution under any circumstances
Deemed to be a criminal offence by the presiding judge
mcqs.answer: Not automatically a nullity for want of jurisdiction merely because it is barred by limitation, though it may be erroneous and open to appeal/revision
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general principle, S.3 interpretation

mcqs.topic: General - Application of S.12 to Applications
mcqs.question: The exclusion of time for obtaining a copy under S.12(2) applies to appeals, applications for leave to appeal, and applications for revision or review of judgment, but as a matter of drafting, it does NOT, by its own terms, automatically extend to:
options: Every kind of miscellaneous application unless the specific Article/provision so provides
Any proceeding whatsoever, without exception
Suits only
Only criminal proceedings
mcqs.answer: Every kind of miscellaneous application unless the specific Article/provision so provides
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.12(2) - scope

mcqs.topic: General - Government Suits
mcqs.question: Historically, certain provisions of the Limitation Act (as inherited from the colonial-era statute) provided a longer period of limitation for suits by or on behalf of the Government as compared to suits by private persons for analogous claims, reflecting the special treatment of:
options: The State/Government as litigant under the Schedule to the Act
Minors exclusively
Foreign nationals exclusively
Corporations exclusively
mcqs.answer: The State/Government as litigant under the Schedule to the Act
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - Schedule I, government suits provision; verify current applicability

mcqs.topic: General - Object of Limitation Law
mcqs.question: The underlying policy/object of the law of limitation, as commonly stated by courts, is that the law assists the vigilant, not those who sleep over their rights, and it aims to:
options: Ensure certainty, finality of litigation, and prevent stale claims, while giving adequate time to pursue genuine rights
Punish plaintiffs for filing suits
Ensure that no suit can ever be dismissed
Protect only defendants, never plaintiffs
mcqs.answer: Ensure certainty, finality of litigation, and prevent stale claims, while giving adequate time to pursue genuine rights
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act - general object and policy

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Balance of Account (Art. 1)
mcqs.question: A suit for the balance due on a mutual, open and current account, where there have been reciprocal demands between the parties, must be filed within what period, and from when does it run?
options: 3 years, from the close of the year in which the last item admitted or proved is entered in the account
1 year, from the date of the first transaction
12 years, from the date of the last transaction only
6 years, from the date the account is closed by mutual consent only
mcqs.answer: 3 years, from the close of the year in which the last item admitted or proved is entered in the account
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I, Art. 1

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Money Payable for Money Found Due on Accounting
mcqs.question: A suit for money payable on an account stated between the parties is governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the stated account
1 year from the date of the stated account
12 years from the date of the stated account
There is no limitation for an account stated
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the stated account
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - account stated

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Money Lent (Art. 19-59 range)
mcqs.question: A suit for money lent, where no time for repayment is fixed, must be brought within 3 years, and time begins to run from:
options: The date the loan is made
The date the lender demands repayment, regardless of when the loan was made
The death of the borrower
There is no limitation for informal loans
mcqs.answer: The date the loan is made
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money lent

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Money Lent Payable on Demand
mcqs.question: Where money is lent under an agreement that it shall be payable on demand, the 3-year limitation period runs from:
options: The date of the loan itself (not the date of demand), as a general rule
The date of demand only, no matter how many years later
The date of the borrower's death
The date the lender files suit
mcqs.answer: The date of the loan itself (not the date of demand), as a general rule
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money lent on demand

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Money Payable for Money Paid on Existing Consideration
mcqs.question: A suit for money paid for the plaintiff's use at the defendant's request must be brought within 3 years, computed from:
options: The date the money is paid
The date the plaintiff makes a demand only
The date the defendant acknowledges verbally
12 years from the date of payment
mcqs.answer: The date the money is paid
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money paid for defendant's use

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Interest on a Loan
mcqs.question: A suit to recover arrears of interest on a loan (not secured by mortgage), which have fallen due and remain unpaid, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the interest becomes due
1 year from when the interest becomes due
6 years from when the loan was advanced
12 years from when the loan was advanced
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the interest becomes due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - interest on loan

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit on a Bond
mcqs.question: A suit upon a bond (other than one for payment of money under a registered deed subject to a longer period) is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date the bond becomes payable
1 year from the date of execution
12 years from the date of execution regardless of the payable date
There is no limitation for suits on bonds
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the bond becomes payable
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit on a bond

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit upon a Registered Instrument for Payment of Money
mcqs.question: Where a suit is founded on a registered instrument securing repayment of money (such as certain registered bonds/mortgage bonds), a longer limitation period generally applies compared to unregistered instruments, reflecting the general policy that:
options: Registered instruments, being more formal and reliable evidence of a solemn undertaking, generally attract longer limitation periods
Registration has no bearing on limitation at all
Registered instruments always attract shorter limitation periods
Registration converts the claim into one for immovable property regardless of subject-matter
mcqs.answer: Registered instruments, being more formal and reliable evidence of a solemn undertaking, generally attract longer limitation periods
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - registered instruments, general principle

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit on a Promissory Note Payable on Demand
mcqs.question: A suit on a promissory note or bond payable on demand, not accompanied by any other instrument, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the instrument
3 years from the date of demand, regardless of when executed
1 year from the date of the instrument
12 years from the date of the instrument
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the instrument
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - promissory note payable on demand

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Price of Goods Sold and Delivered
mcqs.question: A suit for the price of goods sold and delivered, where no fixed period of credit is agreed, must be filed within:
options: 3 years from the date of delivery of the goods
1 year from the date of delivery
12 years from the date of delivery
6 years from the date of delivery
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of delivery of the goods
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - price of goods sold and delivered

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Goods Sold on Credit
mcqs.question: Where goods are sold and delivered on credit, without any fixed period agreed for payment, but the parties intend the price not to be payable until a demand, time begins to run from:
options: The expiration of the credit period agreed (or from delivery if no credit period is fixed)
The date of manufacture of the goods
The date the goods are consumed by the buyer
There is no limitation for credit sales
mcqs.answer: The expiration of the credit period agreed (or from delivery if no credit period is fixed)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - goods sold on credit

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Work Done
mcqs.question: A suit for the price of work done by the plaintiff for the defendant, at his request, where no time is fixed for payment, must be brought within:
options: 3 years from the date the work is done
1 year from the date of the contract
12 years from completion
There is no specific limitation; it falls under the residuary article only
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the work is done
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - price of work done

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Breach of Contract (No Special Period)
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for the breach of any contract, express or implied, not specially provided for elsewhere in the Schedule, is governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the breach
1 year from the date of the breach
6 years from the date of the breach
12 years from the date of the breach
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the breach
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - compensation for breach of contract

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Breach of Contract to Deliver Specific Movable Property
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for breach of a contract to deliver specific movable property, or for a specific chattel, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date fixed for delivery, or if no date is fixed, from the date of demand and refusal
1 year from the date of the contract only
12 years from the date of the contract
There is no limitation for delivery of specific chattels
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date fixed for delivery, or if no date is fixed, from the date of demand and refusal
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - breach of contract to deliver specific movable property

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Wrongful Seizure of Movable Property
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for wrongfully taking or injuring or wrongfully detaining movable property is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
1 year, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
12 years, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
6 years, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
mcqs.answer: 3 years, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - wrongful seizure of movable property

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Compensation for Tort/General Wrong (Residuary Tort Article)
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for any malfeasance, misfeasance, or nonfeasance independent of contract, and not specially provided for elsewhere in the Schedule, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date the act or omission complained of takes place
3 years from the date of the act
12 years from the date of the act
There is no limitation for torts
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the act or omission complained of takes place
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - general tort article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Assault
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for assault or battery is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date of the assault
3 years from the date of the assault
12 years from the date of the assault
6 years from the date of the assault
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date of the assault
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - assault

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Defamation
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for words (slander) or libel is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date the words are spoken or the libel is published
3 years from the date of publication
12 years from the date of publication
There is no limitation for defamation
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the words are spoken or the libel is published
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - defamation

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Malicious Prosecution
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for malicious prosecution is generally governed by a limitation period of 1 year, computed from:
options: The date the plaintiff is acquitted, or the prosecution is otherwise terminated in his favour
The date the prosecution first commenced
The date the defendant lodged the false complaint
The date the plaintiff was arrested
mcqs.answer: The date the plaintiff is acquitted, or the prosecution is otherwise terminated in his favour
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - malicious prosecution

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for False Imprisonment
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for false imprisonment is generally governed by a limitation period of 1 year, running from:
options: The date the plaintiff is released from confinement
The date the imprisonment began
The date judgment is passed in a related criminal case
There is no limitation for false imprisonment
mcqs.answer: The date the plaintiff is released from confinement
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - false imprisonment

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Trespass to Immovable Property
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for trespass on immovable property is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the trespass
1 year from the date of the trespass
12 years from the date of the trespass
6 years from the date of the trespass
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the trespass
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - trespass to immovable property

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Possession by a Person Dispossessed of Immovable Property
mcqs.question: A suit by a person who has been dispossessed of immovable property, and who sues to recover possession based on prior possession alone (not title) as against a person who has no better right, is governed by a limitation period of:
options: 6 years/1 year from the date of dispossession, depending on the specific ground and edition; commonly known as the 'suit on possessory title' provision
12 years always, regardless of the basis of the claim
There is no limitation for a possessory suit
30 years, same as suits based on title
mcqs.answer: 6 years/1 year from the date of dispossession, depending on the specific ground and edition; commonly known as the 'suit on possessory title' provision
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - possessory suit; verify exact period in current bare Act

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Possession of Immovable Property Based on Title
mcqs.question: A suit for possession of immovable property, or any interest therein, not otherwise specially provided for, based on the plaintiff's own title, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff
1 year from the date of dispossession
3 years from the date of dispossession
6 years from the date of dispossession
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for possession based on title

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by a Remainderman/Reversioner for Possession
mcqs.question: A suit for possession of immovable property by a person entitled to possession on the death of a Hindu or Muslim female / holder of a limited estate, brought against a person who has taken possession, is generally computed with limitation running from:
options: The death of the limited owner (life estate holder), not from any earlier adverse possession against the limited owner
The date the original limited estate was created
The birth of the reversioner
There is no limitation for reversioners
mcqs.answer: The death of the limited owner (life estate holder), not from any earlier adverse possession against the limited owner
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit by reversioner; general principle

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Redemption of Mortgage
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagor to redeem, or to recover possession of, immovable property mortgaged is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 60 years, from the date the right to redeem accrues
12 years from the date of the mortgage
3 years from the date of default in payment
30 years from the date of the mortgage deed
mcqs.answer: 60 years, from the date the right to redeem accrues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for redemption of mortgage

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Enforce a Simple Mortgage
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagee (other than a suit for foreclosure or a suit for redemption) to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage of immovable property is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the money sued for becomes due
3 years from the date of the mortgage
60 years from the date of the mortgage
1 year from default
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the money sued for becomes due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit to enforce a mortgage

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Foreclosure
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagee for foreclosure, or a suit by a mortgagor for a decree that a mortgagee do deliver up documents to him, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from when the money secured becomes due
60 years, same as redemption suits
3 years from the mortgage date
1 year from default in payment
mcqs.answer: 12 years from when the money secured becomes due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for foreclosure

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by Mortgagee against Mortgagor to Recover Possession
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagee to recover possession of immovable property mortgaged, where the mortgage is by conditional sale or the like, generally follows the limitation applicable to suits based on:
options: 12 years, akin to suits for possession based on the mortgage title
1 year, treated as a tort claim
3 years, treated as a simple contract claim
There is no limitation for mortgagee possession suits
mcqs.answer: 12 years, akin to suits for possession based on the mortgage title
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - mortgagee's suit for possession

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Partition
mcqs.question: A suit for partition of joint family/co-owned property, where the plaintiff has been excluded from possession, is generally governed by a limitation period reckoned from the date of exclusion, commonly:
options: 12 years from the date the plaintiff is excluded from joint possession or enjoyment
There is no limitation for partition suits so long as the property remains joint
1 year from the date of exclusion
60 years from the date the property was acquired
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the plaintiff is excluded from joint possession or enjoyment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for partition

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Partition Suit where Possession Remains Joint
mcqs.question: Where co-owners remain in joint possession and there has been no exclusion or ouster, the general principle is that the limitation period for a partition suit:
options: Does not begin to run, as possession of one co-owner is possession of all
Begins to run automatically after 12 years from acquisition
Begins to run from the date of the original purchase
Is fixed at exactly 3 years regardless of possession
mcqs.answer: Does not begin to run, as possession of one co-owner is possession of all
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - partition, general principle

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Specific Performance of a Contract
mcqs.question: A suit for specific performance of a contract is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date fixed for performance, or if no date is fixed, from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused
1 year from the date of the contract
12 years from the date of the contract
There is no limitation for specific performance suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date fixed for performance, or if no date is fixed, from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - specific performance

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Rescind a Contract
mcqs.question: A suit to rescind a contract is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to rescind the contract first become known to him
1 year from the date of the contract
12 years from the date of the contract
There is no limitation for rescission suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to rescind the contract first become known to him
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit to rescind a contract

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Cancellation of an Instrument
mcqs.question: A suit to obtain a decree for cancellation of an instrument, not otherwise provided for, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to have the instrument cancelled first become known to him
1 year from the date of execution of the instrument
12 years from the date of registration
60 years from the date of execution
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to have the instrument cancelled first become known to him
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for cancellation of instrument

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Declaration
mcqs.question: A suit to obtain a mere declaration (where no consequential relief is sought or where consequential relief is not otherwise limited), is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the right to sue first accrues
1 year from when the right accrues
12 years from when the right accrues
There is no limitation for declaratory suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the right to sue first accrues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for declaration

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Set Aside a Decree Obtained by Fraud
mcqs.question: A suit to set aside a decree obtained by fraud is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the fraud becomes known to the plaintiff
1 year from the date of the decree
12 years from the date of the decree
There is no limitation once fraud is alleged
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the fraud becomes known to the plaintiff
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit to set aside decree obtained by fraud

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Contribution
mcqs.question: A suit for contribution by a co-obligor (e.g., a co-surety) who has paid more than his share of a common debt is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of payment in excess of the plaintiff's own share
1 year from the date of the original debt
12 years from the date of payment
There is no limitation for contribution claims
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of payment in excess of the plaintiff's own share
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for contribution

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Contribution by a Surety
mcqs.question: A suit by a surety against the principal debtor to recover money paid by the surety on the debtor's behalf is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of payment by the surety
1 year from the date of the guarantee
12 years from the date of the guarantee
60 years from the date of the guarantee
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of payment by the surety
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - surety's suit against principal debtor

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Arrears of Rent
mcqs.question: A suit for arrears of rent is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the arrears become due
1 year from when the arrears become due
12 years from when the arrears become due
There is no limitation for arrears of rent
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the arrears become due
