mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for arrears of rent

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by Landlord to Recover Possession from Tenant
mcqs.question: A suit by a landlord to recover possession from a tenant, after the determination of the tenancy, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the tenancy is determined
1 year from the date of determination
3 years from the date of determination
6 years from the date of determination
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the tenancy is determined
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - landlord's suit to recover possession from tenant

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by Tenant for Enhancement/Reduction of Rent
mcqs.question: Where a special local law (such as a Tenancy Act) prescribes its own period for a suit by a landlord/tenant to modify rent, the Limitation Act, 1908 provisions would apply under:
options: S.29(2), only to the extent not excluded by the special law
S.5 exclusively, with no reference to the special law
The special law is wholly irrelevant to limitation
The residuary Article alone, ignoring the special law
mcqs.answer: S.29(2), only to the extent not excluded by the special law
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.29(2) applied to tenancy suits

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Pre-emption
mcqs.question: A suit to enforce a right of pre-emption is generally governed by a limitation period of 1 year, computed from:
options: The date of the sale sought to be pre-empted becoming known to the plaintiff, or from registration/completion (depending on applicable law)
The date the plaintiff was born
The date the property was originally acquired by the vendor
There is no limitation for pre-emption suits
mcqs.answer: The date of the sale sought to be pre-empted becoming known to the plaintiff, or from registration/completion (depending on applicable law)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for pre-emption

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Dower
mcqs.question: Under the Limitation Act, a Muslim wife's suit to recover prompt dower is generally treated akin to a suit for money due, and limitation for deferred dower typically runs from:
options: The dissolution of marriage by death or divorce
The date of the marriage (nikah) itself in every case
The date the husband remarries
There is no limitation for dower claims
mcqs.answer: The dissolution of marriage by death or divorce
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for dower (Muslim personal law context)

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Maintenance
mcqs.question: A suit to recover arrears of maintenance is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the arrears become due
1 year from when the arrears become due
12 years from when the arrears become due
There is no limitation for maintenance arrears
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the arrears become due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for arrears of maintenance

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by a Ward against Guardian
mcqs.question: A suit by a ward, after attaining majority, to obtain a declaration that a transfer of property made by his guardian, while he was a minor, is voidable, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years from:
options: The date the ward attains majority
The date of the original transfer, regardless of majority
The date the guardian dies
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: The date the ward attains majority
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit by ward against guardian

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Accounts and Share of Profits by a Partner
mcqs.question: A suit for an account and share of profits of a dissolved partnership is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, computed from:
options: The date of the dissolution
The date the partnership was formed
The date of the last profit distribution before dissolution
There is no limitation for partnership accounts
mcqs.answer: The date of the dissolution
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for accounts of dissolved partnership

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit against a Factor/Agent for Accounts
mcqs.question: A suit against a factor, agent, or other person for an account, and a share of profits of a joint venture, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, running from:
options: The termination of the agency/joint venture, or when the account is asked for and refused
The date the agency began
The date of the first transaction
There is no limitation against agents
mcqs.answer: The termination of the agency/joint venture, or when the account is asked for and refused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit against agent for accounts

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Breach of Trust
mcqs.question: As previously noted under S.10, a suit against a trustee (or his representative) to recover trust property, or for breach of an express trust, is generally:
options: Not barred by any period of limitation, as against the trustee holding the trust property
Barred after exactly 3 years
Barred after exactly 12 years
Barred after exactly 1 year
mcqs.answer: Not barred by any period of limitation, as against the trustee holding the trust property
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.10, read with Schedule I

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit against Executor/Administrator for a Legacy
mcqs.question: A suit for a legacy, or for a distributive share of the estate of a deceased person, against an executor or administrator, or some other person legally charged with the duty of distributing it, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from when the legacy or share becomes payable or deliverable
3 years from the date of death of the testator
1 year from the grant of probate
There is no limitation for legacy suits
mcqs.answer: 12 years from when the legacy or share becomes payable or deliverable
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for a legacy

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Movable Property Deposited/Pledged
mcqs.question: A suit for movable property deposited or pledged, and afterwards claimed by the depositor/pledger, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years from:
options: The date the demand for return is refused (or the date the deposit is known to have been converted)
The date of the original deposit only
12 years from the date of deposit
There is no limitation for deposited goods
mcqs.answer: The date the demand for return is refused (or the date the deposit is known to have been converted)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for movable property deposited

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Recover Movable Property Mortgaged and Afterwards Sold
mcqs.question: A suit for movable property mortgaged and afterwards wrongfully sold by the mortgagee before the right of sale accrues to him, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of sale
1 year from the date of sale
12 years from the date of mortgage
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of sale
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - movable property mortgaged and wrongfully sold

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Breach of Warranty of Quality
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for breach of a warranty of quality (e.g., in a contract of sale), unless there is an express warranty of a later date, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years from:
options: The date of sale
The date the goods are consumed
The date of the warranty period expiring only
There is no limitation for breach of warranty
mcqs.answer: The date of sale
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - breach of warranty of quality

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Failure to Deliver Goods
mcqs.question: A suit against a carrier for compensation for non-delivery of, or delay in delivering, goods is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, running from:
options: The date the goods ought to have been delivered
The date the goods were entrusted to the carrier
12 years from entrustment
There is no limitation against carriers
mcqs.answer: The date the goods ought to have been delivered
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit against carrier for non-delivery/delay

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Loss/Injury to Goods by Carrier
mcqs.question: A suit against a carrier for compensation for injury to goods occasioned by the negligence or misconduct of the carrier or his servants is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date the loss or injury occurs
1 year from the date the loss occurs
12 years from the date the loss occurs
There is no limitation for such claims
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the loss or injury occurs
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - carrier's negligence causing loss/injury to goods

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Money Deposited under an Agreement to Repay on Demand
mcqs.question: A suit for money deposited under an agreement that it shall be payable on demand, including money in a bank account, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, running from:
options: The date of the demand made and refused
The date of the deposit itself, always
12 years from the deposit
There is no limitation for bank deposits
mcqs.answer: The date of the demand made and refused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money deposited, repayable on demand

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Recover a Debt Barred by an Award
mcqs.question: A suit to set aside an award, or to enforce an award (in relation to a domestic arbitration), is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years, and time generally runs from the date of the award (or, for setting aside, from when it becomes known to the party)
1 year in every case
12 years in every case
There is no limitation for arbitral awards
mcqs.answer: 3 years, and time generally runs from the date of the award (or, for setting aside, from when it becomes known to the party)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit relating to an award

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit upon a Judgment (Foreign Judgment)
mcqs.question: A suit upon a foreign judgment, treating the judgment itself as the cause of action (subject to it being enforceable), is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 6 years/3 years (varies by edition) from the date of the judgment
1 year from the date of the judgment
There is no limitation for foreign judgments
60 years from the date of the judgment
mcqs.answer: 6 years/3 years (varies by edition) from the date of the judgment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit upon a foreign judgment; verify exact period in current bare Act

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Money Had and Received
mcqs.question: A suit for money had and received by the defendant for the plaintiff's use is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, running from:
options: The date the money is received
The date the plaintiff first requests an account
12 years from receipt
There is no limitation for such claims
mcqs.answer: The date the money is received
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money had and received

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Immovable Property from a Trespasser
mcqs.question: A suit for possession of immovable property when the plaintiff has been dispossessed without title (by a trespasser having no better right), where the plaintiff relies on prior possession, is generally governed by a limitation period of (commonly) 12 years, and the possession of the trespasser becomes 'adverse' from:
options: The date of dispossession/trespass, subject to the nature of the trespasser's continued possession
The date the plaintiff acquires knowledge, regardless of possession
The date the property is registered in the trespasser's name
There is no limitation for suits against trespassers
mcqs.answer: The date of dispossession/trespass, subject to the nature of the trespasser's continued possession
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit against trespasser for possession

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for a Loss Suffered by a Public Officer's Wrongful Act
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for an act done in pursuance of the execution or intended execution of, or in respect of any alleged neglect or default in the execution of, any statutory duty by a public officer is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date of the act, neglect, or default complained of
3 years from the date of the act
12 years from the date of the act
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date of the act, neglect, or default complained of
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit against public officer for acts done in official duty

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Injunction
mcqs.question: A suit for a perpetual injunction, when not otherwise governed by a specific article, is generally governed under the residuary article, meaning the period is:
options: 3 years, from when the right to sue first accrues
1 year, treated as a tort claim in every case
12 years, treated as a possession claim in every case
There is no limitation for injunction suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years, from when the right to sue first accrues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary article for suits not otherwise provided

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Residuary Article (Suits Not Otherwise Provided For)
mcqs.question: The 'residuary article' of Schedule I (First Division), applicable to a suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in the Schedule, prescribes a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the right to sue accrues
1 year from when the right to sue accrues
6 years from when the right to sue accrues
12 years from when the right to sue accrues
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the right to sue accrues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary article (commonly cited as Art. 120)

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Residuary Article, When Applied
mcqs.question: The residuary article of the First Division applies only when:
options: No other specific article in the Schedule covers the particular suit
The suit is filed by the government
The suit relates to immovable property only
The court has inherent jurisdiction over the matter
mcqs.answer: No other specific article in the Schedule covers the particular suit
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary article, interpretation

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Suit for Balance of Mutual Account
mcqs.question: A shopkeeper and a customer maintain a mutual, open, running account with reciprocal transactions from 2018 to 2023. The last entry admitted by both is dated 15 March 2023. A suit for the balance due must ordinarily be filed within:
options: 3 years from the close of the year in which the last item (15 March 2023) is entered
3 years from 2018, when the account was first opened
1 year from 2023
There is no limitation as the account was mutual
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the close of the year in which the last item (15 March 2023) is entered
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I, Art. 1 - application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Loan Repayable on Demand
mcqs.question: A lends Tk. 50,000 to B on 1 January 2020, repayable 'on demand'. A makes no demand until 1 January 2025. As a general rule, limitation for A's suit to recover the loan runs:
options: From 1 January 2020 (the date of the loan), so the suit filed in 2025 would ordinarily be time-barred absent any acknowledgment/part-payment
From 1 January 2025 (the date of demand), so the suit is well within time
There is no limitation for demand loans
From the date B dies, regardless of demand
mcqs.answer: From 1 January 2020 (the date of the loan), so the suit filed in 2025 would ordinarily be time-barred absent any acknowledgment/part-payment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money lent, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Adverse Possession Suit
mcqs.question: X's land is trespassed upon and occupied openly, continuously, and hostilely by Y starting 1 January 2005, without any permission from X. X files a suit for possession on 1 January 2018. Applying the 12-year period for suits based on title (and considering S.27), X's suit is:
options: Time-barred, and X's title to the land stands extinguished under S.27
Well within time, since immovable property suits never get barred
Time-barred only as to remedy, but X's title still survives fully
Governed by the 1-year tort period, so barred even earlier
mcqs.answer: Time-barred, and X's title to the land stands extinguished under S.27
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I read with S.27 - application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Suit for Specific Performance
mcqs.question: A contract for sale of land fixes 1 June 2022 as the date for registration of the sale deed. The vendor refuses to execute on that date. The purchaser files a suit for specific performance on 1 June 2026. Applying the 3-year period (from the date fixed for performance), the suit is:
options: Time-barred, as more than 3 years have elapsed since 1 June 2022
Within time, as specific performance suits have no limitation
Within time, since the 12-year period for immovable property applies instead
Time-barred only if the purchaser was in possession
mcqs.answer: Time-barred, as more than 3 years have elapsed since 1 June 2022
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - specific performance, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Suit for Defamation
mcqs.question: A newspaper publishes a defamatory article about P on 1 January 2024. P wishes to file a civil suit for damages. Applying the 1-year period for defamation, P must file by:
options: 1 January 2025
1 January 2027 (3 years)
1 January 2036 (12 years)
There is no limitation for defamation suits
mcqs.answer: 1 January 2025
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - defamation, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Mortgage Redemption
mcqs.question: A mortgagor executes a mortgage deed on 1 January 1980 with no fixed redemption date issue arising until default. Given the 60-year period for redemption suits, a redemption suit filed in 2030 would ordinarily be:
options: Within time, since the 60-year period (subject to when the right to redeem accrues) has not expired
Time-barred, since more than 12 years have passed
Time-barred, since more than 3 years have passed
Governed by the residuary 3-year article instead
mcqs.answer: Within time, since the 60-year period (subject to when the right to redeem accrues) has not expired
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for redemption of mortgage, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Rent Arrears
mcqs.question: A tenant fails to pay rent for the months of January to June 2023. The landlord files a suit for these arrears in January 2027. Applying the 3-year period for arrears of rent, the suit for the January-June 2023 arrears is:
options: Time-barred, as more than 3 years have elapsed since the rent became due
Within time, since rent suits follow the 12-year immovable property period
Within time, since there is no limitation for rent
Governed by S.22 (continuing breach) so it never becomes barred
mcqs.answer: Time-barred, as more than 3 years have elapsed since the rent became due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for arrears of rent, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Suit for Price of Goods with Credit Period
mcqs.question: A sells goods to B on 1 January 2023 on 6 months' credit (i.e., payable by 1 July 2023). B does not pay. A's 3-year limitation period to sue for the price begins from:
options: 1 July 2023 (expiry of the credit period), not from 1 January 2023
1 January 2023 (date of delivery), regardless of the credit period
The date A finally demands payment, however late
There is no limitation for sale of goods
mcqs.answer: 1 July 2023 (expiry of the credit period), not from 1 January 2023
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - goods sold on credit, application

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Breach of Contract to Marry
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for breach of a promise/contract to marry is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date the promise is broken
1 year from the date of the promise
12 years from the date of the promise
There is no limitation for breach of promise to marry
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the promise is broken
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - breach of promise to marry

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Immovable Property from a Government Grantee
mcqs.question: As a general principle historically applicable, suits by or against the Government regarding immovable property, or suits based on Government grants, could attract a longer limitation period (commonly 30 years) than ordinary private suits based on title (12 years), reflecting:
options: The special protection historically extended to Government/Crown grants under the Schedule
No difference at all between Government and private suits
A shorter period for the Government compared to private persons
Total exemption of the Government from all limitation provisions
mcqs.answer: The special protection historically extended to Government/Crown grants under the Schedule
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - government grants; verify current applicability post-1971

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Injury to Right of Way (Easement)
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for obstruction to a right of way or other easement is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 2 years from the date of obstruction
1 year from the date of obstruction
12 years from the date of obstruction
There is no limitation for easement obstruction
mcqs.answer: 2 years from the date of obstruction
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - obstruction to easement

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Profits of Immovable Property Belonging to Plaintiff Wrongfully Received by Defendant
mcqs.question: A suit for profits of immovable property belonging to the plaintiff, which have been wrongfully received by the defendant, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, from:
options: When the profits are received
When the plaintiff first acquires the property
12 years from receipt, treating it as an immovable property claim
There is no limitation for wrongful receipt of profits
mcqs.answer: When the profits are received
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for wrongfully received profits

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Arrears of an Annuity/Charge on Immovable Property
mcqs.question: A suit to recover arrears of an annuity, or other periodical charge, chargeable upon immovable property (not being rent), is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from when the arrears become due
3 years from when the arrears become due
1 year from when the arrears become due
There is no limitation for such charges
mcqs.answer: 12 years from when the arrears become due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - arrears of annuity/charge

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Contribution among Co-Sharers Regarding Common Expenses
mcqs.question: A suit for contribution by a co-sharer of immovable property who has paid more than his share of common expenses (such as revenue) is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of payment
12 years from the date of payment
1 year from the date of payment
There is no limitation for such contribution
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of payment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - contribution among co-sharers

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of a Fine/Penalty under a Contract
mcqs.question: A suit for the recovery of a penalty (not being a penalty payable to the Government) under a contract is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from when the penalty is incurred
3 years from when the penalty is incurred
12 years from when the penalty is incurred
There is no limitation for penalties
mcqs.answer: 1 year from when the penalty is incurred
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - recovery of a penalty

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Money Payable under an Award Where No Suit Is Brought to Enforce It
mcqs.question: In respect of an unregistered award to which the Arbitration law applies, treating it as creating a fresh cause of action for the sum awarded, the general limitation period applicable is:
options: 3 years from the date the award is made (or communicated), subject to the specific arbitration law provisions
12 years from the date of the underlying dispute
1 year from the date the award is made
There is no limitation for enforcing awards
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the award is made (or communicated), subject to the specific arbitration law provisions
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit on an award; verify against Arbitration Act provisions

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Inducing Breach of Contract
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for wrongfully inducing another to break a contract with the plaintiff is generally governed under the general tort residuary period of:
options: 1 year from the date the contract is broken
3 years from the date of the inducement
12 years from the date of the inducement
There is no limitation for such a tort
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the contract is broken
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - tort of inducing breach of contract

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Movable Property, No Contract Involved
mcqs.question: A suit for the recovery of specific movable property, or in the alternative for its value, when the property has been wrongfully taken and not been mortgaged, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date the property is taken
1 year from the date the property is taken
12 years from the date the property is taken
There is no limitation for movable property recovery
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the property is taken
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for recovery of specific movable property

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit under Personal Law for Restitution of Conjugal Rights
mcqs.question: A suit for restitution of conjugal rights is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 2 years from the date of the refusal to cohabit
1 year from the date of marriage
12 years from the date of marriage
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: 2 years from the date of the refusal to cohabit
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for restitution of conjugal rights

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for a Share of Joint Family Property
mcqs.question: Where a member of a joint family is excluded from the enjoyment of joint family property and sues for his share, this is generally treated akin to a partition suit and governed by the:
options: 12-year period from the date of exclusion
3-year residuary period from the date of exclusion
1-year tort period from exclusion
There is no limitation as family property is inalienable
mcqs.answer: 12-year period from the date of exclusion
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - joint family property/partition analogy

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Recover Possession of Immovable Property Sold in Execution of a Decree
mcqs.question: A suit by a judgment-debtor (or a person claiming under him) to recover possession of immovable property sold in execution of a decree, on the ground that the sale is void or the auction-purchaser's title is defective, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the property is sold, or a shorter special period depending on the specific ground of challenge
3 years in every case
1 year in every case
There is no limitation for challenging execution sales
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the property is sold, or a shorter special period depending on the specific ground of challenge
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit to recover property sold in execution

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Set Aside an Execution Sale on the Ground of Irregularity
mcqs.question: An application to set aside a sale in execution of a decree on the ground of a material irregularity or fraud in publishing/conducting the sale is generally governed by a short limitation period of:
options: 30 days (or a similarly short period) from the date of sale, being an application rather than a suit
3 years, being treated as a suit
12 years, being treated as a suit for possession
There is no limitation for challenging irregularities
mcqs.answer: 30 days (or a similarly short period) from the date of sale, being an application rather than a suit
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I (Applications) read with Order XXI Rule 90 CPC

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for a Perpetual Injunction to Restrain a Continuing Breach
mcqs.question: Where the wrong sought to be restrained by injunction is a continuing wrong (e.g., ongoing encroachment), the limitation period for the injunction suit, applying S.22, effectively:
options: Runs afresh from each continuing act, so long as the wrong continues
Is fixed permanently from the very first act of encroachment, with no renewal
Never applies since injunctions are always available
Is governed exclusively by the 60-year mortgage period
mcqs.answer: Runs afresh from each continuing act, so long as the wrong continues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.22 read with Schedule I residuary article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Breach of a Covenant/Condition of a Lease
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for breach of a covenant or condition contained in a lease is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the breach
1 year from the date of the lease
12 years from the date of the lease
There is no limitation for lease covenant breaches
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the breach
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - breach of covenant/condition of a lease

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for the Diversion of a Watercourse
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for diverting a watercourse, or for wrongful use of water flowing in a defined channel, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 2 years from the date of the diversion/wrongful use
1 year from the date of diversion
12 years from the date of diversion
There is no limitation for such claims
mcqs.answer: 2 years from the date of the diversion/wrongful use
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - diversion of watercourse

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for the Profits of an Office
mcqs.question: A suit to recover the profits/emoluments of an office wrongfully withheld is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the profits are received by the defendant (or when payment is refused to the plaintiff)
1 year from the date the plaintiff loses office
12 years from the date the plaintiff loses office
There is no limitation for office emoluments
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the profits are received by the defendant (or when payment is refused to the plaintiff)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - profits of an office

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Wrongful Dismissal from Office
mcqs.question: A suit for wrongful dismissal from public office, or for a declaration that the dismissal is void, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date of the dismissal
3 years from the date of dismissal
12 years from the date of dismissal
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date of the dismissal
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for wrongful dismissal

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Seduction
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for seduction of the plaintiff's wife/daughter (as recognized under older common-law-influenced provisions) is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date of the act complained of
3 years from the date of the act
12 years from the date of the act
There is no limitation for such an action
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date of the act complained of
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - historical tort provision; verify continued applicability

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Contribution between Co-Sureties
mcqs.question: A suit for contribution between co-sureties, where one surety has paid more than his share, generally follows the same principle as contribution among co-obligors, with limitation running from:
options: The date the paying surety discharges more than his own share of the liability
The date the original guarantee was executed
The date the principal debtor defaults, regardless of payment
There is no limitation between co-sureties
mcqs.answer: The date the paying surety discharges more than his own share of the liability
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - contribution between co-sureties

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Possession by a Purchaser at a Court Sale
mcqs.question: A suit by an auction-purchaser at a court sale (execution sale) for possession of the property purchased, against a person in wrongful possession, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the sale becomes absolute (or from dispossession, per specific facts)
3 years from the date of the sale
1 year from the date of the sale
There is no limitation for court-auction purchasers
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the sale becomes absolute (or from dispossession, per specific facts)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - auction purchaser's suit for possession

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation Where No Special Period Provided (Contract vs Tort Distinction)
mcqs.question: In deciding whether the 3-year (contract) or the 1-year (tort) residuary period applies to an unusual claim, courts examine primarily whether the claim is founded:
options: In contract (breach of an obligation arising from agreement) or in tort (an independent civil wrong)
On the value of the claim in money terms
On whether the defendant is a government employee
On the number of witnesses available
mcqs.answer: In contract (breach of an obligation arising from agreement) or in tort (an independent civil wrong)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - contract vs tort residuary, interpretation

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for a Debt Not Otherwise Provided For
mcqs.question: Where a suit for recovery of a debt does not fall precisely within any specific article (e.g., money lent, price of goods, etc.), it generally falls back on:
options: The 3-year residuary article for suits founded on contract
The 1-year residuary article for torts
The 12-year period for immovable property
The 60-year period for mortgage redemption
mcqs.answer: The 3-year residuary article for suits founded on contract
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary contract article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Negligence (Non-Contractual)
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for injury caused by the defendant's negligence, where no contract exists between the parties, is generally governed by the general tort residuary period of:
options: 1 year from the date the injury is caused
3 years from the date of injury
12 years from the date of injury
There is no limitation for negligence claims
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the injury is caused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - general tort residuary article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Injuries Caused by Animals
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for injury caused by the defendant's animal, straying or otherwise causing damage, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date the injury is caused
3 years from the date of injury
12 years from the date of injury
There is no limitation for injury caused by animals
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the injury is caused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - tort by animal, general residuary tort article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Immovable Property by a Mortgagor after Foreclosure
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagor to recover possession of mortgaged immovable property after the mortgagee has obtained a decree for foreclosure, on grounds such as fraud in obtaining the decree, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years, or a shorter period if a specific ground (e.g., fraud) attracts a different article
3 years in every case, without exception
1 year in every case
There is no limitation once foreclosure is decreed
mcqs.answer: 12 years, or a shorter period if a specific ground (e.g., fraud) attracts a different article
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - mortgagor's suit after foreclosure

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Recover Possession from a Co-Sharer/Mortgagee in Possession
mcqs.question: A suit by a co-sharer to recover his share of joint property from another co-sharer or a mortgagee in possession is generally treated akin to a suit for possession based on title, and thus governed (as a general rule) by:
options: The 12-year limitation period, running from ouster or exclusion
The 3-year residuary contract period
The 1-year tort period
There is no limitation as between co-sharers
mcqs.answer: The 12-year limitation period, running from ouster or exclusion
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - co-sharer's suit for possession

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Choosing Contract vs Residuary Article
mcqs.question: A hires B to paint his house for a fixed sum, payable on completion, but no completion date is fixed. B never completes the work. A wishes to sue for damages. The limitation period applicable, and its starting point, would most likely be:
options: 3 years, from the date B is called upon to complete and fails, or from when the breach becomes apparent
1 year, treating it purely as a tort claim
12 years, treating it as an immovable property claim since a house is involved
There is no limitation since no completion date was fixed
mcqs.answer: 3 years, from the date B is called upon to complete and fails, or from when the breach becomes apparent
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - contract for work, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Applying the Residuary Article
mcqs.question: A right accrues to P on 1 January 2022 to bring a suit for which no specific article in Schedule I applies (e.g., a novel equitable claim). Applying the residuary article, P must ordinarily file suit by:
options: 1 January 2025 (3 years from accrual of the right to sue)
1 January 2023 (1 year from accrual)
1 January 2034 (12 years from accrual)
There is no deadline since no specific article applies
mcqs.answer: 1 January 2025 (3 years from accrual of the right to sue)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary article, application

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Balance of Account (Art. 1)
mcqs.question: A suit for the balance due on a mutual, open and current account, where there have been reciprocal demands between the parties, must be filed within what period, and from when does it run?
options: 3 years, from the close of the year in which the last item admitted or proved is entered in the account
1 year, from the date of the first transaction
12 years, from the date of the last transaction only
6 years, from the date the account is closed by mutual consent only
mcqs.answer: 3 years, from the close of the year in which the last item admitted or proved is entered in the account
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I, Art. 1

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Money Payable for Money Found Due on Accounting
mcqs.question: A suit for money payable on an account stated between the parties is governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the stated account
1 year from the date of the stated account
12 years from the date of the stated account
There is no limitation for an account stated
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the stated account
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - account stated

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Money Lent (Art. 19-59 range)
mcqs.question: A suit for money lent, where no time for repayment is fixed, must be brought within 3 years, and time begins to run from:
options: The date the loan is made
The date the lender demands repayment, regardless of when the loan was made
The death of the borrower
There is no limitation for informal loans
mcqs.answer: The date the loan is made
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money lent

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Money Lent Payable on Demand
mcqs.question: Where money is lent under an agreement that it shall be payable on demand, the 3-year limitation period runs from:
options: The date of the loan itself (not the date of demand), as a general rule
The date of demand only, no matter how many years later
The date of the borrower's death
The date the lender files suit
mcqs.answer: The date of the loan itself (not the date of demand), as a general rule
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money lent on demand

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Money Payable for Money Paid on Existing Consideration
mcqs.question: A suit for money paid for the plaintiff's use at the defendant's request must be brought within 3 years, computed from:
options: The date the money is paid
The date the plaintiff makes a demand only
The date the defendant acknowledges verbally
12 years from the date of payment
mcqs.answer: The date the money is paid
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money paid for defendant's use

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Interest on a Loan
mcqs.question: A suit to recover arrears of interest on a loan (not secured by mortgage), which have fallen due and remain unpaid, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the interest becomes due
1 year from when the interest becomes due
6 years from when the loan was advanced
12 years from when the loan was advanced
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the interest becomes due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - interest on loan

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit on a Bond
mcqs.question: A suit upon a bond (other than one for payment of money under a registered deed subject to a longer period) is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date the bond becomes payable
1 year from the date of execution
12 years from the date of execution regardless of the payable date
There is no limitation for suits on bonds
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the bond becomes payable
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit on a bond

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit upon a Registered Instrument for Payment of Money
mcqs.question: Where a suit is founded on a registered instrument securing repayment of money (such as certain registered bonds/mortgage bonds), a longer limitation period generally applies compared to unregistered instruments, reflecting the general policy that:
options: Registered instruments, being more formal and reliable evidence of a solemn undertaking, generally attract longer limitation periods
Registration has no bearing on limitation at all
Registered instruments always attract shorter limitation periods
Registration converts the claim into one for immovable property regardless of subject-matter
mcqs.answer: Registered instruments, being more formal and reliable evidence of a solemn undertaking, generally attract longer limitation periods
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - registered instruments, general principle

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit on a Promissory Note Payable on Demand
mcqs.question: A suit on a promissory note or bond payable on demand, not accompanied by any other instrument, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the instrument
3 years from the date of demand, regardless of when executed
1 year from the date of the instrument
12 years from the date of the instrument
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the instrument
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - promissory note payable on demand

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Price of Goods Sold and Delivered
mcqs.question: A suit for the price of goods sold and delivered, where no fixed period of credit is agreed, must be filed within:
options: 3 years from the date of delivery of the goods
1 year from the date of delivery
12 years from the date of delivery
6 years from the date of delivery
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of delivery of the goods
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - price of goods sold and delivered

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Goods Sold on Credit
mcqs.question: Where goods are sold and delivered on credit, without any fixed period agreed for payment, but the parties intend the price not to be payable until a demand, time begins to run from:
options: The expiration of the credit period agreed (or from delivery if no credit period is fixed)
The date of manufacture of the goods
The date the goods are consumed by the buyer
There is no limitation for credit sales
mcqs.answer: The expiration of the credit period agreed (or from delivery if no credit period is fixed)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - goods sold on credit

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Work Done
mcqs.question: A suit for the price of work done by the plaintiff for the defendant, at his request, where no time is fixed for payment, must be brought within:
options: 3 years from the date the work is done
1 year from the date of the contract
12 years from completion
There is no specific limitation; it falls under the residuary article only
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the work is done
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - price of work done

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Breach of Contract (No Special Period)
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for the breach of any contract, express or implied, not specially provided for elsewhere in the Schedule, is governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the breach
1 year from the date of the breach
6 years from the date of the breach
12 years from the date of the breach
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the breach
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - compensation for breach of contract

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Breach of Contract to Deliver Specific Movable Property
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for breach of a contract to deliver specific movable property, or for a specific chattel, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date fixed for delivery, or if no date is fixed, from the date of demand and refusal
1 year from the date of the contract only
12 years from the date of the contract
There is no limitation for delivery of specific chattels
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date fixed for delivery, or if no date is fixed, from the date of demand and refusal
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - breach of contract to deliver specific movable property

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Wrongful Seizure of Movable Property
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for wrongfully taking or injuring or wrongfully detaining movable property is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
1 year, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
12 years, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
6 years, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
mcqs.answer: 3 years, from the date of the seizure/injury/detention
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - wrongful seizure of movable property

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Compensation for Tort/General Wrong (Residuary Tort Article)
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for any malfeasance, misfeasance, or nonfeasance independent of contract, and not specially provided for elsewhere in the Schedule, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date the act or omission complained of takes place
3 years from the date of the act
12 years from the date of the act
There is no limitation for torts
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the act or omission complained of takes place
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - general tort article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Assault
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for assault or battery is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date of the assault
3 years from the date of the assault
12 years from the date of the assault
6 years from the date of the assault
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date of the assault
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - assault

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Defamation
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for words (slander) or libel is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date the words are spoken or the libel is published
3 years from the date of publication
12 years from the date of publication
There is no limitation for defamation
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the words are spoken or the libel is published
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - defamation

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Malicious Prosecution
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for malicious prosecution is generally governed by a limitation period of 1 year, computed from:
options: The date the plaintiff is acquitted, or the prosecution is otherwise terminated in his favour
The date the prosecution first commenced
The date the defendant lodged the false complaint
The date the plaintiff was arrested
mcqs.answer: The date the plaintiff is acquitted, or the prosecution is otherwise terminated in his favour
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - malicious prosecution

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for False Imprisonment
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for false imprisonment is generally governed by a limitation period of 1 year, running from:
options: The date the plaintiff is released from confinement
The date the imprisonment began
The date judgment is passed in a related criminal case
There is no limitation for false imprisonment
mcqs.answer: The date the plaintiff is released from confinement
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - false imprisonment

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Trespass to Immovable Property
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for trespass on immovable property is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the trespass
1 year from the date of the trespass
12 years from the date of the trespass
6 years from the date of the trespass
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the trespass
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - trespass to immovable property

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Possession by a Person Dispossessed of Immovable Property
mcqs.question: A suit by a person who has been dispossessed of immovable property, and who sues to recover possession based on prior possession alone (not title) as against a person who has no better right, is governed by a limitation period of:
options: 6 years/1 year from the date of dispossession, depending on the specific ground and edition; commonly known as the 'suit on possessory title' provision
12 years always, regardless of the basis of the claim
There is no limitation for a possessory suit
30 years, same as suits based on title
mcqs.answer: 6 years/1 year from the date of dispossession, depending on the specific ground and edition; commonly known as the 'suit on possessory title' provision
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - possessory suit; verify exact period in current bare Act

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Possession of Immovable Property Based on Title
mcqs.question: A suit for possession of immovable property, or any interest therein, not otherwise specially provided for, based on the plaintiff's own title, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff
1 year from the date of dispossession
3 years from the date of dispossession
6 years from the date of dispossession
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for possession based on title

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by a Remainderman/Reversioner for Possession
mcqs.question: A suit for possession of immovable property by a person entitled to possession on the death of a Hindu or Muslim female / holder of a limited estate, brought against a person who has taken possession, is generally computed with limitation running from:
options: The death of the limited owner (life estate holder), not from any earlier adverse possession against the limited owner
The date the original limited estate was created
The birth of the reversioner
There is no limitation for reversioners
mcqs.answer: The death of the limited owner (life estate holder), not from any earlier adverse possession against the limited owner
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit by reversioner; general principle

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Redemption of Mortgage
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagor to redeem, or to recover possession of, immovable property mortgaged is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 60 years, from the date the right to redeem accrues
12 years from the date of the mortgage
3 years from the date of default in payment
30 years from the date of the mortgage deed
mcqs.answer: 60 years, from the date the right to redeem accrues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for redemption of mortgage

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Enforce a Simple Mortgage
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagee (other than a suit for foreclosure or a suit for redemption) to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage of immovable property is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the money sued for becomes due
3 years from the date of the mortgage
60 years from the date of the mortgage
1 year from default
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the money sued for becomes due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit to enforce a mortgage

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Foreclosure
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagee for foreclosure, or a suit by a mortgagor for a decree that a mortgagee do deliver up documents to him, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from when the money secured becomes due
60 years, same as redemption suits
3 years from the mortgage date
1 year from default in payment
mcqs.answer: 12 years from when the money secured becomes due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for foreclosure

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by Mortgagee against Mortgagor to Recover Possession
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagee to recover possession of immovable property mortgaged, where the mortgage is by conditional sale or the like, generally follows the limitation applicable to suits based on:
options: 12 years, akin to suits for possession based on the mortgage title
1 year, treated as a tort claim
3 years, treated as a simple contract claim
There is no limitation for mortgagee possession suits
mcqs.answer: 12 years, akin to suits for possession based on the mortgage title
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - mortgagee's suit for possession

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Partition
mcqs.question: A suit for partition of joint family/co-owned property, where the plaintiff has been excluded from possession, is generally governed by a limitation period reckoned from the date of exclusion, commonly:
options: 12 years from the date the plaintiff is excluded from joint possession or enjoyment
There is no limitation for partition suits so long as the property remains joint
1 year from the date of exclusion
60 years from the date the property was acquired
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the plaintiff is excluded from joint possession or enjoyment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for partition

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Partition Suit where Possession Remains Joint
mcqs.question: Where co-owners remain in joint possession and there has been no exclusion or ouster, the general principle is that the limitation period for a partition suit:
options: Does not begin to run, as possession of one co-owner is possession of all
Begins to run automatically after 12 years from acquisition
Begins to run from the date of the original purchase
Is fixed at exactly 3 years regardless of possession
mcqs.answer: Does not begin to run, as possession of one co-owner is possession of all
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - partition, general principle

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Specific Performance of a Contract
mcqs.question: A suit for specific performance of a contract is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date fixed for performance, or if no date is fixed, from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused
1 year from the date of the contract
12 years from the date of the contract
There is no limitation for specific performance suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date fixed for performance, or if no date is fixed, from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - specific performance

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Rescind a Contract
mcqs.question: A suit to rescind a contract is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to rescind the contract first become known to him
1 year from the date of the contract
12 years from the date of the contract
There is no limitation for rescission suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to rescind the contract first become known to him
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit to rescind a contract

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Cancellation of an Instrument
mcqs.question: A suit to obtain a decree for cancellation of an instrument, not otherwise provided for, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to have the instrument cancelled first become known to him
1 year from the date of execution of the instrument
12 years from the date of registration
60 years from the date of execution
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to have the instrument cancelled first become known to him
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for cancellation of instrument

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Declaration
mcqs.question: A suit to obtain a mere declaration (where no consequential relief is sought or where consequential relief is not otherwise limited), is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the right to sue first accrues
1 year from when the right accrues
12 years from when the right accrues
There is no limitation for declaratory suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the right to sue first accrues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for declaration

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Set Aside a Decree Obtained by Fraud
mcqs.question: A suit to set aside a decree obtained by fraud is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the fraud becomes known to the plaintiff
1 year from the date of the decree
12 years from the date of the decree
There is no limitation once fraud is alleged
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the fraud becomes known to the plaintiff
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit to set aside decree obtained by fraud

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Contribution
mcqs.question: A suit for contribution by a co-obligor (e.g., a co-surety) who has paid more than his share of a common debt is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of payment in excess of the plaintiff's own share
1 year from the date of the original debt
12 years from the date of payment
There is no limitation for contribution claims
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of payment in excess of the plaintiff's own share
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for contribution

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Contribution by a Surety
mcqs.question: A suit by a surety against the principal debtor to recover money paid by the surety on the debtor's behalf is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of payment by the surety
1 year from the date of the guarantee
12 years from the date of the guarantee
60 years from the date of the guarantee
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of payment by the surety
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - surety's suit against principal debtor

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Arrears of Rent
mcqs.question: A suit for arrears of rent is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the arrears become due
1 year from when the arrears become due
12 years from when the arrears become due
There is no limitation for arrears of rent
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the arrears become due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for arrears of rent

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by Landlord to Recover Possession from Tenant
mcqs.question: A suit by a landlord to recover possession from a tenant, after the determination of the tenancy, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the tenancy is determined
1 year from the date of determination
3 years from the date of determination
6 years from the date of determination
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the tenancy is determined
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - landlord's suit to recover possession from tenant

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by Tenant for Enhancement/Reduction of Rent
mcqs.question: Where a special local law (such as a Tenancy Act) prescribes its own period for a suit by a landlord/tenant to modify rent, the Limitation Act, 1908 provisions would apply under:
options: S.29(2), only to the extent not excluded by the special law
S.5 exclusively, with no reference to the special law
The special law is wholly irrelevant to limitation
The residuary Article alone, ignoring the special law
mcqs.answer: S.29(2), only to the extent not excluded by the special law
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.29(2) applied to tenancy suits

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Pre-emption
mcqs.question: A suit to enforce a right of pre-emption is generally governed by a limitation period of 1 year, computed from:
options: The date of the sale sought to be pre-empted becoming known to the plaintiff, or from registration/completion (depending on applicable law)
The date the plaintiff was born
The date the property was originally acquired by the vendor
There is no limitation for pre-emption suits
mcqs.answer: The date of the sale sought to be pre-empted becoming known to the plaintiff, or from registration/completion (depending on applicable law)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for pre-emption

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Dower
mcqs.question: Under the Limitation Act, a Muslim wife's suit to recover prompt dower is generally treated akin to a suit for money due, and limitation for deferred dower typically runs from:
options: The dissolution of marriage by death or divorce
The date of the marriage (nikah) itself in every case
The date the husband remarries
There is no limitation for dower claims
mcqs.answer: The dissolution of marriage by death or divorce
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for dower (Muslim personal law context)

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Maintenance
mcqs.question: A suit to recover arrears of maintenance is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the arrears become due
1 year from when the arrears become due
12 years from when the arrears become due
There is no limitation for maintenance arrears
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the arrears become due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for arrears of maintenance

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit by a Ward against Guardian
mcqs.question: A suit by a ward, after attaining majority, to obtain a declaration that a transfer of property made by his guardian, while he was a minor, is voidable, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years from:
options: The date the ward attains majority
The date of the original transfer, regardless of majority
The date the guardian dies
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: The date the ward attains majority
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit by ward against guardian

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Accounts and Share of Profits by a Partner
mcqs.question: A suit for an account and share of profits of a dissolved partnership is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, computed from:
options: The date of the dissolution
The date the partnership was formed
The date of the last profit distribution before dissolution
There is no limitation for partnership accounts
mcqs.answer: The date of the dissolution
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for accounts of dissolved partnership

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit against a Factor/Agent for Accounts
mcqs.question: A suit against a factor, agent, or other person for an account, and a share of profits of a joint venture, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, running from:
options: The termination of the agency/joint venture, or when the account is asked for and refused
The date the agency began
The date of the first transaction
There is no limitation against agents
mcqs.answer: The termination of the agency/joint venture, or when the account is asked for and refused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit against agent for accounts

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Breach of Trust
mcqs.question: As previously noted under S.10, a suit against a trustee (or his representative) to recover trust property, or for breach of an express trust, is generally:
options: Not barred by any period of limitation, as against the trustee holding the trust property
Barred after exactly 3 years
Barred after exactly 12 years
Barred after exactly 1 year
mcqs.answer: Not barred by any period of limitation, as against the trustee holding the trust property
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.10, read with Schedule I

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit against Executor/Administrator for a Legacy
mcqs.question: A suit for a legacy, or for a distributive share of the estate of a deceased person, against an executor or administrator, or some other person legally charged with the duty of distributing it, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from when the legacy or share becomes payable or deliverable
3 years from the date of death of the testator
1 year from the grant of probate
There is no limitation for legacy suits
mcqs.answer: 12 years from when the legacy or share becomes payable or deliverable
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for a legacy

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Movable Property Deposited/Pledged
mcqs.question: A suit for movable property deposited or pledged, and afterwards claimed by the depositor/pledger, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years from:
options: The date the demand for return is refused (or the date the deposit is known to have been converted)
The date of the original deposit only
12 years from the date of deposit
There is no limitation for deposited goods
mcqs.answer: The date the demand for return is refused (or the date the deposit is known to have been converted)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for movable property deposited

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Recover Movable Property Mortgaged and Afterwards Sold
mcqs.question: A suit for movable property mortgaged and afterwards wrongfully sold by the mortgagee before the right of sale accrues to him, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of sale
1 year from the date of sale
12 years from the date of mortgage
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of sale
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - movable property mortgaged and wrongfully sold

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Breach of Warranty of Quality
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for breach of a warranty of quality (e.g., in a contract of sale), unless there is an express warranty of a later date, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years from:
options: The date of sale
The date the goods are consumed
The date of the warranty period expiring only
There is no limitation for breach of warranty
mcqs.answer: The date of sale
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - breach of warranty of quality

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Failure to Deliver Goods
mcqs.question: A suit against a carrier for compensation for non-delivery of, or delay in delivering, goods is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, running from:
options: The date the goods ought to have been delivered
The date the goods were entrusted to the carrier
12 years from entrustment
There is no limitation against carriers
mcqs.answer: The date the goods ought to have been delivered
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit against carrier for non-delivery/delay

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Loss/Injury to Goods by Carrier
mcqs.question: A suit against a carrier for compensation for injury to goods occasioned by the negligence or misconduct of the carrier or his servants is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date the loss or injury occurs
1 year from the date the loss occurs
12 years from the date the loss occurs
There is no limitation for such claims
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the loss or injury occurs
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - carrier's negligence causing loss/injury to goods

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Money Deposited under an Agreement to Repay on Demand
mcqs.question: A suit for money deposited under an agreement that it shall be payable on demand, including money in a bank account, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, running from:
options: The date of the demand made and refused
The date of the deposit itself, always
12 years from the deposit
There is no limitation for bank deposits
mcqs.answer: The date of the demand made and refused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money deposited, repayable on demand

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Recover a Debt Barred by an Award
mcqs.question: A suit to set aside an award, or to enforce an award (in relation to a domestic arbitration), is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years, and time generally runs from the date of the award (or, for setting aside, from when it becomes known to the party)
1 year in every case
12 years in every case
There is no limitation for arbitral awards
mcqs.answer: 3 years, and time generally runs from the date of the award (or, for setting aside, from when it becomes known to the party)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit relating to an award

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit upon a Judgment (Foreign Judgment)
mcqs.question: A suit upon a foreign judgment, treating the judgment itself as the cause of action (subject to it being enforceable), is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 6 years/3 years (varies by edition) from the date of the judgment
1 year from the date of the judgment
There is no limitation for foreign judgments
60 years from the date of the judgment
mcqs.answer: 6 years/3 years (varies by edition) from the date of the judgment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit upon a foreign judgment; verify exact period in current bare Act

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Money Had and Received
mcqs.question: A suit for money had and received by the defendant for the plaintiff's use is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, running from:
options: The date the money is received
The date the plaintiff first requests an account
12 years from receipt
There is no limitation for such claims
mcqs.answer: The date the money is received
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money had and received

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Immovable Property from a Trespasser
mcqs.question: A suit for possession of immovable property when the plaintiff has been dispossessed without title (by a trespasser having no better right), where the plaintiff relies on prior possession, is generally governed by a limitation period of (commonly) 12 years, and the possession of the trespasser becomes 'adverse' from:
options: The date of dispossession/trespass, subject to the nature of the trespasser's continued possession
The date the plaintiff acquires knowledge, regardless of possession
The date the property is registered in the trespasser's name
There is no limitation for suits against trespassers
mcqs.answer: The date of dispossession/trespass, subject to the nature of the trespasser's continued possession
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit against trespasser for possession

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for a Loss Suffered by a Public Officer's Wrongful Act
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for an act done in pursuance of the execution or intended execution of, or in respect of any alleged neglect or default in the execution of, any statutory duty by a public officer is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date of the act, neglect, or default complained of
3 years from the date of the act
12 years from the date of the act
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date of the act, neglect, or default complained of
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit against public officer for acts done in official duty

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Injunction
mcqs.question: A suit for a perpetual injunction, when not otherwise governed by a specific article, is generally governed under the residuary article, meaning the period is:
options: 3 years, from when the right to sue first accrues
1 year, treated as a tort claim in every case
12 years, treated as a possession claim in every case
There is no limitation for injunction suits
mcqs.answer: 3 years, from when the right to sue first accrues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary article for suits not otherwise provided

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Residuary Article (Suits Not Otherwise Provided For)
mcqs.question: The 'residuary article' of Schedule I (First Division), applicable to a suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in the Schedule, prescribes a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the right to sue accrues
1 year from when the right to sue accrues
6 years from when the right to sue accrues
12 years from when the right to sue accrues
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the right to sue accrues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary article (commonly cited as Art. 120)

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Residuary Article, When Applied
mcqs.question: The residuary article of the First Division applies only when:
options: No other specific article in the Schedule covers the particular suit
The suit is filed by the government
The suit relates to immovable property only
The court has inherent jurisdiction over the matter
mcqs.answer: No other specific article in the Schedule covers the particular suit
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary article, interpretation

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Suit for Balance of Mutual Account
mcqs.question: A shopkeeper and a customer maintain a mutual, open, running account with reciprocal transactions from 2018 to 2023. The last entry admitted by both is dated 15 March 2023. A suit for the balance due must ordinarily be filed within:
options: 3 years from the close of the year in which the last item (15 March 2023) is entered
3 years from 2018, when the account was first opened
1 year from 2023
There is no limitation as the account was mutual
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the close of the year in which the last item (15 March 2023) is entered
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I, Art. 1 - application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Loan Repayable on Demand
mcqs.question: A lends Tk. 50,000 to B on 1 January 2020, repayable 'on demand'. A makes no demand until 1 January 2025. As a general rule, limitation for A's suit to recover the loan runs:
options: From 1 January 2020 (the date of the loan), so the suit filed in 2025 would ordinarily be time-barred absent any acknowledgment/part-payment
From 1 January 2025 (the date of demand), so the suit is well within time
There is no limitation for demand loans
From the date B dies, regardless of demand
mcqs.answer: From 1 January 2020 (the date of the loan), so the suit filed in 2025 would ordinarily be time-barred absent any acknowledgment/part-payment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - money lent, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Adverse Possession Suit
mcqs.question: X's land is trespassed upon and occupied openly, continuously, and hostilely by Y starting 1 January 2005, without any permission from X. X files a suit for possession on 1 January 2018. Applying the 12-year period for suits based on title (and considering S.27), X's suit is:
options: Time-barred, and X's title to the land stands extinguished under S.27
Well within time, since immovable property suits never get barred
Time-barred only as to remedy, but X's title still survives fully
Governed by the 1-year tort period, so barred even earlier
mcqs.answer: Time-barred, and X's title to the land stands extinguished under S.27
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I read with S.27 - application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Suit for Specific Performance
mcqs.question: A contract for sale of land fixes 1 June 2022 as the date for registration of the sale deed. The vendor refuses to execute on that date. The purchaser files a suit for specific performance on 1 June 2026. Applying the 3-year period (from the date fixed for performance), the suit is:
options: Time-barred, as more than 3 years have elapsed since 1 June 2022
Within time, as specific performance suits have no limitation
Within time, since the 12-year period for immovable property applies instead
Time-barred only if the purchaser was in possession
mcqs.answer: Time-barred, as more than 3 years have elapsed since 1 June 2022
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - specific performance, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Suit for Defamation
mcqs.question: A newspaper publishes a defamatory article about P on 1 January 2024. P wishes to file a civil suit for damages. Applying the 1-year period for defamation, P must file by:
options: 1 January 2025
1 January 2027 (3 years)
1 January 2036 (12 years)
There is no limitation for defamation suits
mcqs.answer: 1 January 2025
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - defamation, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Mortgage Redemption
