mcqs.question: A mortgagor executes a mortgage deed on 1 January 1980 with no fixed redemption date issue arising until default. Given the 60-year period for redemption suits, a redemption suit filed in 2030 would ordinarily be:
options: Within time, since the 60-year period (subject to when the right to redeem accrues) has not expired
Time-barred, since more than 12 years have passed
Time-barred, since more than 3 years have passed
Governed by the residuary 3-year article instead
mcqs.answer: Within time, since the 60-year period (subject to when the right to redeem accrues) has not expired
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for redemption of mortgage, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Rent Arrears
mcqs.question: A tenant fails to pay rent for the months of January to June 2023. The landlord files a suit for these arrears in January 2027. Applying the 3-year period for arrears of rent, the suit for the January-June 2023 arrears is:
options: Time-barred, as more than 3 years have elapsed since the rent became due
Within time, since rent suits follow the 12-year immovable property period
Within time, since there is no limitation for rent
Governed by S.22 (continuing breach) so it never becomes barred
mcqs.answer: Time-barred, as more than 3 years have elapsed since the rent became due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for arrears of rent, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Suit for Price of Goods with Credit Period
mcqs.question: A sells goods to B on 1 January 2023 on 6 months' credit (i.e., payable by 1 July 2023). B does not pay. A's 3-year limitation period to sue for the price begins from:
options: 1 July 2023 (expiry of the credit period), not from 1 January 2023
1 January 2023 (date of delivery), regardless of the credit period
The date A finally demands payment, however late
There is no limitation for sale of goods
mcqs.answer: 1 July 2023 (expiry of the credit period), not from 1 January 2023
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - goods sold on credit, application

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Breach of Contract to Marry
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for breach of a promise/contract to marry is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date the promise is broken
1 year from the date of the promise
12 years from the date of the promise
There is no limitation for breach of promise to marry
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the promise is broken
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - breach of promise to marry

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Immovable Property from a Government Grantee
mcqs.question: As a general principle historically applicable, suits by or against the Government regarding immovable property, or suits based on Government grants, could attract a longer limitation period (commonly 30 years) than ordinary private suits based on title (12 years), reflecting:
options: The special protection historically extended to Government/Crown grants under the Schedule
No difference at all between Government and private suits
A shorter period for the Government compared to private persons
Total exemption of the Government from all limitation provisions
mcqs.answer: The special protection historically extended to Government/Crown grants under the Schedule
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - government grants; verify current applicability post-1971

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Injury to Right of Way (Easement)
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for obstruction to a right of way or other easement is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 2 years from the date of obstruction
1 year from the date of obstruction
12 years from the date of obstruction
There is no limitation for easement obstruction
mcqs.answer: 2 years from the date of obstruction
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - obstruction to easement

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Profits of Immovable Property Belonging to Plaintiff Wrongfully Received by Defendant
mcqs.question: A suit for profits of immovable property belonging to the plaintiff, which have been wrongfully received by the defendant, is generally governed by a limitation period of 3 years, from:
options: When the profits are received
When the plaintiff first acquires the property
12 years from receipt, treating it as an immovable property claim
There is no limitation for wrongful receipt of profits
mcqs.answer: When the profits are received
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for wrongfully received profits

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Arrears of an Annuity/Charge on Immovable Property
mcqs.question: A suit to recover arrears of an annuity, or other periodical charge, chargeable upon immovable property (not being rent), is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from when the arrears become due
3 years from when the arrears become due
1 year from when the arrears become due
There is no limitation for such charges
mcqs.answer: 12 years from when the arrears become due
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - arrears of annuity/charge

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Contribution among Co-Sharers Regarding Common Expenses
mcqs.question: A suit for contribution by a co-sharer of immovable property who has paid more than his share of common expenses (such as revenue) is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of payment
12 years from the date of payment
1 year from the date of payment
There is no limitation for such contribution
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of payment
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - contribution among co-sharers

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of a Fine/Penalty under a Contract
mcqs.question: A suit for the recovery of a penalty (not being a penalty payable to the Government) under a contract is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from when the penalty is incurred
3 years from when the penalty is incurred
12 years from when the penalty is incurred
There is no limitation for penalties
mcqs.answer: 1 year from when the penalty is incurred
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - recovery of a penalty

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Money Payable under an Award Where No Suit Is Brought to Enforce It
mcqs.question: In respect of an unregistered award to which the Arbitration law applies, treating it as creating a fresh cause of action for the sum awarded, the general limitation period applicable is:
options: 3 years from the date the award is made (or communicated), subject to the specific arbitration law provisions
12 years from the date of the underlying dispute
1 year from the date the award is made
There is no limitation for enforcing awards
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the award is made (or communicated), subject to the specific arbitration law provisions
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit on an award; verify against Arbitration Act provisions

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Inducing Breach of Contract
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for wrongfully inducing another to break a contract with the plaintiff is generally governed under the general tort residuary period of:
options: 1 year from the date the contract is broken
3 years from the date of the inducement
12 years from the date of the inducement
There is no limitation for such a tort
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the contract is broken
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - tort of inducing breach of contract

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Movable Property, No Contract Involved
mcqs.question: A suit for the recovery of specific movable property, or in the alternative for its value, when the property has been wrongfully taken and not been mortgaged, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date the property is taken
1 year from the date the property is taken
12 years from the date the property is taken
There is no limitation for movable property recovery
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date the property is taken
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for recovery of specific movable property

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit under Personal Law for Restitution of Conjugal Rights
mcqs.question: A suit for restitution of conjugal rights is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 2 years from the date of the refusal to cohabit
1 year from the date of marriage
12 years from the date of marriage
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: 2 years from the date of the refusal to cohabit
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for restitution of conjugal rights

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for a Share of Joint Family Property
mcqs.question: Where a member of a joint family is excluded from the enjoyment of joint family property and sues for his share, this is generally treated akin to a partition suit and governed by the:
options: 12-year period from the date of exclusion
3-year residuary period from the date of exclusion
1-year tort period from exclusion
There is no limitation as family property is inalienable
mcqs.answer: 12-year period from the date of exclusion
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - joint family property/partition analogy

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Recover Possession of Immovable Property Sold in Execution of a Decree
mcqs.question: A suit by a judgment-debtor (or a person claiming under him) to recover possession of immovable property sold in execution of a decree, on the ground that the sale is void or the auction-purchaser's title is defective, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the property is sold, or a shorter special period depending on the specific ground of challenge
3 years in every case
1 year in every case
There is no limitation for challenging execution sales
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the property is sold, or a shorter special period depending on the specific ground of challenge
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit to recover property sold in execution

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Set Aside an Execution Sale on the Ground of Irregularity
mcqs.question: An application to set aside a sale in execution of a decree on the ground of a material irregularity or fraud in publishing/conducting the sale is generally governed by a short limitation period of:
options: 30 days (or a similarly short period) from the date of sale, being an application rather than a suit
3 years, being treated as a suit
12 years, being treated as a suit for possession
There is no limitation for challenging irregularities
mcqs.answer: 30 days (or a similarly short period) from the date of sale, being an application rather than a suit
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I (Applications) read with Order XXI Rule 90 CPC

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for a Perpetual Injunction to Restrain a Continuing Breach
mcqs.question: Where the wrong sought to be restrained by injunction is a continuing wrong (e.g., ongoing encroachment), the limitation period for the injunction suit, applying S.22, effectively:
options: Runs afresh from each continuing act, so long as the wrong continues
Is fixed permanently from the very first act of encroachment, with no renewal
Never applies since injunctions are always available
Is governed exclusively by the 60-year mortgage period
mcqs.answer: Runs afresh from each continuing act, so long as the wrong continues
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, S.22 read with Schedule I residuary article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Breach of a Covenant/Condition of a Lease
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for breach of a covenant or condition contained in a lease is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from the date of the breach
1 year from the date of the lease
12 years from the date of the lease
There is no limitation for lease covenant breaches
mcqs.answer: 3 years from the date of the breach
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - breach of covenant/condition of a lease

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for the Diversion of a Watercourse
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for diverting a watercourse, or for wrongful use of water flowing in a defined channel, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 2 years from the date of the diversion/wrongful use
1 year from the date of diversion
12 years from the date of diversion
There is no limitation for such claims
mcqs.answer: 2 years from the date of the diversion/wrongful use
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - diversion of watercourse

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for the Profits of an Office
mcqs.question: A suit to recover the profits/emoluments of an office wrongfully withheld is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 3 years from when the profits are received by the defendant (or when payment is refused to the plaintiff)
1 year from the date the plaintiff loses office
12 years from the date the plaintiff loses office
There is no limitation for office emoluments
mcqs.answer: 3 years from when the profits are received by the defendant (or when payment is refused to the plaintiff)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - profits of an office

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Wrongful Dismissal from Office
mcqs.question: A suit for wrongful dismissal from public office, or for a declaration that the dismissal is void, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date of the dismissal
3 years from the date of dismissal
12 years from the date of dismissal
There is no limitation for such suits
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date of the dismissal
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - suit for wrongful dismissal

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Seduction
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for seduction of the plaintiff's wife/daughter (as recognized under older common-law-influenced provisions) is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date of the act complained of
3 years from the date of the act
12 years from the date of the act
There is no limitation for such an action
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date of the act complained of
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - historical tort provision; verify continued applicability

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Contribution between Co-Sureties
mcqs.question: A suit for contribution between co-sureties, where one surety has paid more than his share, generally follows the same principle as contribution among co-obligors, with limitation running from:
options: The date the paying surety discharges more than his own share of the liability
The date the original guarantee was executed
The date the principal debtor defaults, regardless of payment
There is no limitation between co-sureties
mcqs.answer: The date the paying surety discharges more than his own share of the liability
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - contribution between co-sureties

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Possession by a Purchaser at a Court Sale
mcqs.question: A suit by an auction-purchaser at a court sale (execution sale) for possession of the property purchased, against a person in wrongful possession, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years from the date the sale becomes absolute (or from dispossession, per specific facts)
3 years from the date of the sale
1 year from the date of the sale
There is no limitation for court-auction purchasers
mcqs.answer: 12 years from the date the sale becomes absolute (or from dispossession, per specific facts)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - auction purchaser's suit for possession

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation Where No Special Period Provided (Contract vs Tort Distinction)
mcqs.question: In deciding whether the 3-year (contract) or the 1-year (tort) residuary period applies to an unusual claim, courts examine primarily whether the claim is founded:
options: In contract (breach of an obligation arising from agreement) or in tort (an independent civil wrong)
On the value of the claim in money terms
On whether the defendant is a government employee
On the number of witnesses available
mcqs.answer: In contract (breach of an obligation arising from agreement) or in tort (an independent civil wrong)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - contract vs tort residuary, interpretation

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for a Debt Not Otherwise Provided For
mcqs.question: Where a suit for recovery of a debt does not fall precisely within any specific article (e.g., money lent, price of goods, etc.), it generally falls back on:
options: The 3-year residuary article for suits founded on contract
The 1-year residuary article for torts
The 12-year period for immovable property
The 60-year period for mortgage redemption
mcqs.answer: The 3-year residuary article for suits founded on contract
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary contract article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Negligence (Non-Contractual)
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for injury caused by the defendant's negligence, where no contract exists between the parties, is generally governed by the general tort residuary period of:
options: 1 year from the date the injury is caused
3 years from the date of injury
12 years from the date of injury
There is no limitation for negligence claims
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the injury is caused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - general tort residuary article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Compensation for Injuries Caused by Animals
mcqs.question: A suit for compensation for injury caused by the defendant's animal, straying or otherwise causing damage, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 1 year from the date the injury is caused
3 years from the date of injury
12 years from the date of injury
There is no limitation for injury caused by animals
mcqs.answer: 1 year from the date the injury is caused
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - tort by animal, general residuary tort article

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit for Recovery of Immovable Property by a Mortgagor after Foreclosure
mcqs.question: A suit by a mortgagor to recover possession of mortgaged immovable property after the mortgagee has obtained a decree for foreclosure, on grounds such as fraud in obtaining the decree, is generally governed by a limitation period of:
options: 12 years, or a shorter period if a specific ground (e.g., fraud) attracts a different article
3 years in every case, without exception
1 year in every case
There is no limitation once foreclosure is decreed
mcqs.answer: 12 years, or a shorter period if a specific ground (e.g., fraud) attracts a different article
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - mortgagor's suit after foreclosure

mcqs.topic: Schedule I - Suit to Recover Possession from a Co-Sharer/Mortgagee in Possession
mcqs.question: A suit by a co-sharer to recover his share of joint property from another co-sharer or a mortgagee in possession is generally treated akin to a suit for possession based on title, and thus governed (as a general rule) by:
options: The 12-year limitation period, running from ouster or exclusion
The 3-year residuary contract period
The 1-year tort period
There is no limitation as between co-sharers
mcqs.answer: The 12-year limitation period, running from ouster or exclusion
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - co-sharer's suit for possession

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Choosing Contract vs Residuary Article
mcqs.question: A hires B to paint his house for a fixed sum, payable on completion, but no completion date is fixed. B never completes the work. A wishes to sue for damages. The limitation period applicable, and its starting point, would most likely be:
options: 3 years, from the date B is called upon to complete and fails, or from when the breach becomes apparent
1 year, treating it purely as a tort claim
12 years, treating it as an immovable property claim since a house is involved
There is no limitation since no completion date was fixed
mcqs.answer: 3 years, from the date B is called upon to complete and fails, or from when the breach becomes apparent
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - contract for work, application

mcqs.topic: Scenario - Applying the Residuary Article
mcqs.question: A right accrues to P on 1 January 2022 to bring a suit for which no specific article in Schedule I applies (e.g., a novel equitable claim). Applying the residuary article, P must ordinarily file suit by:
options: 1 January 2025 (3 years from accrual of the right to sue)
1 January 2023 (1 year from accrual)
1 January 2034 (12 years from accrual)
There is no deadline since no specific article applies
mcqs.answer: 1 January 2025 (3 years from accrual of the right to sue)
mcqs.reference: Limitation Act, Schedule I - residuary article, application
